1.1 Brief Description
• Parthandlingwith PERMAS
Theabilitytousepartsasindependentcomputationalmodelsisatechnologytospeed-up
the analysis process especially during the design layout phase, where a lot of modifica-
tionsoccurinashorttimeframe. Theavailablefunctionalityissubsequentlysummarized
briefly.
– Independentmodellingofparts
withouttheneedformatchingmeshesatthe interface.
– Fast changecycle ofvirtualprototypes
Studies of different design variants are highly accelerated, leading to a better feed-
back in thelayout designphase.
– Accurate mesh transition withoutbadelements
by concentratingthetransition to a smallregion.
– Basedon incompatiblemeshes
– Fixed couplingfor linesandsurfaces
– Weld coupling
– Contact
• Substructure Analysis
In addition to the part handling described above, PERMAS allows the decomposition of
a model into substructures. Substructures can be assembled the same way as single
elements and are therefore often called superelements. The assembly process may be
performed on an arbitrary numberof levels. The mostimportantadvantagesof this anal-
ysis techniqueinclude:
– Generally, any substructure may be arbitrarily large and complex, thus allowing the
overall model to assume a size which has so far been impossible in practical appli-
cations.
– Decomposition into substructures is good way to cope with large analysis projects.
Anysubstructuremaybeconstructedandverifiedseparatelybeforeitisinsertedinto
the model.
– Elements may be used on every substructure level, i. e. they may be introduced
even in assembledcomponents.
– Identical substructures may be inserted repeatedly — thus leading to considerable
savings in computationtime.
– Much computationtime mayalso besaved as faras designvariations ornon–linear
analyses are concerned, provided that the modifications respectively the iterations
can be concentratedonto oneof severalsubstructures.
• ElementTypes
PERMASincludescomprehensiveelementfamiliesofferinga widerangeofelementsfor
all fieldsofapplication:
– more than 50 elementtypes for static and dynamic calculations including linearand
nonlinearspring anddamperelements.
– nonlinearshells

– threedimensionalgasketelements
– plotelementsfor visualization purposes
– morethan40elementtypes forheattransfer calculations
– axisymmetric elementsforharmonicanalyses
– specificelementtypesforperformingcalculationsoffluidsandtheircouplingtostruc-
turalelements.
– semi-infinite elementsforelectromagneticoracoustic problems.
– radiatingboundaryconditionelements.

• ModelSize in Calculationswith PERMAS
Thedatamanagementandthebuilt–insolutionalgorithminPERMASaresuitableforthe

analysis,modelsofthis size maybe builtup ofsubstructures thatare simple andeasyto
handle. Suchlargemodelscanalwaysbecalculatedoncomputersystemsofanysize—
onworkstations aswell ason servers. Theonly limitationsare the performance anddisk
storage capacity of the computer system available and the time available for performing
theanalysis.

facilities. In particular, the analysis tools available (e. g. for matrix calculation) may be
applied for flexible in–house user requirements. For standard applications a comfortable
commandlanguage— the UserControlInterface (UCI)— isavailable.

1.2 Basic Definitions
1.2 Basic Definitions
1.2.1 Components and Configurations
The component is an environment for the administration and analysis of a physical system. It
correspondstothefiniteelementmodeloftheentirephysicalsystemorofapartofthesystem.
Thatisingeneral,thecomponentcorrespondsto thefiniteelementmodelinthepreprocessor.
A componentis identifiedbya name,see page3-5.
Contentsofacomponentarethemeshdefinition,boundaryconditionsandloads,thedefinition
and assignmentof physical propertiesand the assignmentof material data. Furthermore defi-
nitions for parameter and topology optimization may belong to a component. The definition of
materialdatais completelyindependentofthe componentdescription.
To each component a discretization type is assigned, which may be discrete (default), or ax-
isymmetric. The discretization type defines the way how the physical system is represented.
In discrete components, all structural elements are useable, but no axisymmetric or Fourier
elements. In axisymmetric componentsonlyaxisymmetric orFourierelementsmay beused.
In order to perform analyses in different physical domains (e.g. mechanical, thermal, etc.) a
componentmay carry different degreeof freedom types, see page1-22. They are selected by
the DOFTYPEparameter. Bydefault,mechanicaldegreesoffreedomare available.
Using the substructure technique,componentsmay be assembled to a so called configuration
(see figure F1-1) in order to model a more complex physical system. Dependent on their
position in such anassembly, thereare severaltypes ofcomponents:
Basic Component: (single component) is a component that is no longer divided into
subcomponents.
Subcomponent: is a componentwhich maybeinsertedinto anothercomponent.
AssembledComponent: (hypercomponent)is a component thatis made upof subcompo-
nents.
TopComponent: is the highestcomponentin the assemblyhierarchy.
Since each component is independent from any other one, the model description (e.g. node
numbers,elements,loads)maybedoneinacompletelyindependentway. Thecouplingpoints
are identified by the definition of external degrees of freedom in the subcomponent and the
correspondingconnectivity definition in thehypercomponent.
A configuration defines the range of componentsto be analyzed in the current computation. It
is identifiedby the nameof the highestcomponentin the assembly hierarchy. This component
is called the top component. The simplest case of a configuration is a single component,
wherethe componentcorrespondsto theconfiguration. A componentmaybea partofseveral
configurations.
Figure F1-1 shows an example for a simple configuration. The configuration is defined by
activating componentCOMP_5as the top component. All subsequentcomputationsare after-
V 19.00.287 PERMASUser’s ReferenceManual(EDU) 1-7
Intro
1 Introduction to PERMAS
wards performed within this configuration. There are no restrictions concerning the number of
componentlevels orthe numberofcomponentsofa configuration.

1.2.2 Variants and Situations
PERMASoffers the possibility to provide inputfor different variants of a modeland to examine
them withinonecalculation.
Invariant data of the model description are collected in the so-called structure bracket. The
main contentsof thestructure bracket are:
• nodalpointcoordinates
• elementtopology
• elementandnodesets
• referencecoordinatesystems
• globalrotated nodebasis definitions
(i.e. assignmentofdisplacementcoordinatesystems)
• invariantlinearmultipointconstraints
Variantsmaybedefinedwith respectto boundaryconditions,loading,physical properties,ma-
terial assignment and other attributes of the model. Variants are indentified by a name. They
can be seen as a container to organize data by their physical meaning. The following types of
variants are available:

ortnI
1.2 Basic Definitions
System Variant: Holds a set of physical properties and related data. The most important
contentsare:
• elementpropertydefinitionsandassignments
• materialassignments(notdefinitions!)
• elementlocalsystems
• globaldampingparameters
ConstraintVariant: Thevariantcontainsa specific set ofboundaryconditions,mainly:
• suppresseddegreesoffreedom
• prescribed degreesoffreedom
• linearmultipointconstraints
• coefficients ofgenerallinearmultipointconstraints
• local system definitions indicating a rotated node basis (displace-
mentcoordinatesystem).
• contactboundaryconditions
LoadingVariant: Serves to organize different loading conditions, e.g. in case of different
constraint variants or several dynamic load cases. One loading variant
maycontain anarbitrarynumberofstatic loadcases.
ModificationVariant: Contains data related to design optimization, like design constraints, de-
sign variable limits orthe like.
ResultVariant: Holds the specification of result requests (e.g. excitation frequencies,
load steps) and the definition of references to existing results (e.g. result
combinationrules).
Thesecontentsareallowedforeach componentlevel(basic orassembledcomponent).
Aspecificcombinationofvariantsforwhichananalysisisperformediscalledasituation. Asitu-
ationisidentifiedbyanameandisthemainlinkbetweenmodeldescriptionandanalysiscontrol.

1.2 Basic Definitions
1.2.3 Coordinate Systems
PERMASsupportsthefollowingcoordinatesystems:
1. The component system is a cartesian coordinate system within each substructure. It
serves asthe referencefor allothercoordinatesystems ofthe component.
2. Reference systems may be used for coordinate input, the transformation of nodal point
vector quantitiesandthe definitionofa rotatednodebasis orlocalelementsystems.
3. The rotatednodebasis is an optional cartesian coordinate system assigned to a nodal
pointtomodifythedirectionsofthedegreesoffreedom. Alsooftencalledadisplacement
coordinatesystem oranalysis coordinatesystem.
The Component System
Each component carries a basic coordinate system, called the component system. The com-
ponentsystem isthe defaultfor:
1. the specification ofnodalpointcoordinates
2. the outputofnodalresultvectors
3. the directionsofthe degreesoffreedom
Reference Systems
In the structure bracket of each component,an arbitrary numberof reference systems may be
defined as local coordinate systems. The reference systems may be cartesian, cylindrical or
spherical coordinate systems. Also special purpose conical, helical and toroidal coordinate
systems areavailable. Theycan beused:
1. for the definitionoffurtherreference coordinatesystems
2. as referencesystems forcoordinates
3. for the definitionofa rotatednodebasis.
4. for the orientationoflocalelementsystems
A reference system is defined by three points, either by specification of nodal point identifiers
orby specification oftheircoordinates(which may referto a referencesystem, too).

1.2 Basic Definitions
Rotated Node Basis
Many applications require the possibility to define the loads and boundary conditions in di-
rections other than the directions given by the component system. For that purpose a local
cartesian coordinate system may be assigned to each node. In PERMAS this coordinate sys-
tem is called rotated node basis. Other terms are displacement coordinate system or analysis
coordinatesystem. Thereare severalpossibilities todefinea rotatednodebasis,see $ROTB:
• Aglobalrotatedbasismaybedefinedwiththe$ROTBstatementinthestructure bracket.
Thisdefinitionis valid for allvariants ofthemodel.
• A variable rotated basis may be defined within the constraint variant using the $ROTB
statement. The freedom directions defined by this way may vary from constraint variant
to constraint variant.
• In both cases the definition may be performed by reference to a reference coordinate
system orbydirect inputofa cartesian system forthe correspondingnode.
Thedefinitionofa rotatednodebasismustbe in accordancewith the followingrules :
1. If reference is made to a cylindrical or spherical system, the local x-axis at the node is
build from the radius vector. Hence this system may not be assigned to nodes on the
z-axis ofa cylindrical or in theorigin ofa sphericalreference system.
2. If a node carries external degrees of freedom, only a global rotated basis may be as-
signed.
3. Aduplicatedefinitionofarotatedbasisatanodeisimpossible. Especiallythe(global)ro-
tated basisofsubcomponentsmust notbedefinedagainonhyper-componentlevel. The
definition is automatically taken over from the subcomponentto the hyper-component. It
isnotallowedtospecifythelocalsystemonhyper-componentlevelforsuchnodes,since
the localsystem is transportedonlyin a bottom-upway.
4. If a hyper-component node which was inserted via $SUBCOMP shall be assigned an
additional local system (and no rotated basis already exists), this may be done in the
constraint bracket.

1 Introduction to PERMAS
1.2.4 Degrees of Freedom, Freedom Classes
Degrees of freedom are the state variables of a discrete system (i.e. finite element model).
PERMAS provides different degree of freedom types for the different classes of physical prob-
lems to besolved:
DISP mechanicalanalyses
POTE electro-magneticanalyses
PRES acoustic analyses
TEMP thermalanalyses
MATH optimizationandcoupledanalyses
A componentmay carry several degree of freedom types in order to perform combined analy-
ses.
The number of degrees of freedom at a particular node is determined by the elements (or
multipoint constraint conditions) which are connected to that node and the degree of freedom
type.
Degree of Freedom Type DISP
The degrees of freedom define the potential movementsof a nodal point as well as the forces
that can be applied at that node. Thus, with each discrete degree of freedom a force and a
displacement vector component are associated that have the same direction in space. This
direction is defined by the node basis that assigns a direction to the corresponding degree of
freedom. Thedefaultdirectionsofthedegreesoffreedomcoincidewiththecomponentsystem.
Nevertheless,anyother direction may be definedby assigning a rotated nodebasis to a nodal
point.

Degree of Freedom Type POTE
The degree of freedom type for electromagnetic calculations is POTE. It is a potential of
four, composed of a vector potential A and a scalar potential φ . For details see the
ExamplesManual.

1.2 Basic Definitions
Freedom Classes
Forallnodalpointorientedmatrices,thenumberofdegreesoffreedomatanodeisdetermined
bythehighestpossibledegreeoffreedominacomponentinordertohavearegularpartitioning
ofthematrices. Sincethesedegreesoffreedomarenotalwaysactuallyexisting ateachnode,
theyare called potentialdegreesoffreedom.
Theactualdegreesoffreedomare those degreesof freedomwhich are elastically supported.
In contrast, degrees of freedom which are not elastically supported are called redundant de-
greesoffreedom. Theymust besuppressedexplicitly.
Theactualdegreesoffreedomarepartitionedinternallyintodisjointfreedomclasses. Thefree-
dom classes are definedbyboundaryconditions(like suppressionof a degreeof freedom,as-
signmentofaprescribedvalue)whicharedefinedwithinaconstraintvariant($CONSTRAINTS)
or by linear constraint equations ($MPC). All degrees of freedom which are not explicitly as-
signed are called local degrees of freedom. The following table shows the freedom classes in
PERMASandtheirdescription.
Class Statement Explanation
L - Localdegreesoffreedom(usuallyno explicit definition)
E $EXTERNAL External degrees of freedom. Coupling degrees of freedom
in a substructure analysis. The definition is done within the
structure bracket.
P $PRESCRIBE Prescribed degrees of freedom. The definition is done within the
constraintvariant,thevaluesforeachloadingpatternaredefinedin
theloadingvariant.
S $SUPPRESS Suppressed degrees of freedom are specified in the
constraintvariant.
D $MPC Dependent degrees of freedom are declared with the DPDOFS-
parameter of the $MPC statement within the structure bracket or
constraintvariant.
Each actual degree of freedom may be assigned to any freedom class. This assignmentmust
beunique,i.e. adegreeoffreedomcanonlybe memberof oneclass.
PERMASdistinguishesbetweendegreesoffreedomwhicharetotallysuppressedanddegrees
offreedomwhichhaveassignedaspecific(prescribed)value. SuppressedDOFsareneglected
when solving the system of equations, whereas prescribed DOFs are a part of the right hand
side (load vector). This allows to solve multiple load patterns with different prescribed values
with a single decompositionofthe system matrix.

Central Data Management
PERMASconvertsallinputdata(preprocessorfiles,PERMASinputfiles)intoaninternalformat
and stores them on a database. This database is available during the analysis process as
backingstorage. Inthisdatabase,resultsaswellasinterimresultsarestored. Itmaybesaved
andusedfor subsequentruns.
All read– and write–operations from this database to the central memory and vice versa are
controlled and monitored by a core management program (Data Object ManagementSystem
DMS),thatiscomparabletoanoperatingsystem. Thesize ofthecentralmemorymanagedby
DMS is a dynamic quantity, chosen by the user. Its size is limited to 8GB for the D64 version
and only by the operating system for the S64 version. The database and the central memory
are divided into fixed–size–records (= pages). The typical page size is 512 kilobytes (D64) or
1024 kilobyte (S64). Its optimum value is hardware specific, since it depends on the ratio of
CPUspeed to I/O speed. Thedatabase size mayvary — dependingonthe projectvolume —
from a few megabytes up to several terabytes. Only the pages currently required are loaded
into the centralmemorybyDMS.Thus,merelythe necessarydisk accesses take place.
The communication between PERMAS and the database is made via data objects. A data
objectis definedby:
• the structure ofthe data
• the possible operationsonthe object
• the access functions
PERMASsupportsthefollowingdataobjects:
1. tables
2. sequences
3. books
Tables and sequences serve to store the input data and control information. Books are used
to store matrices, e.g. the nodalcoordinates, loads and displacements. The experienced user
maymanipulatethe books,e.g. byextracting specific information from thedatabaseforfurther
processing.

1.4.1 Structure of the Input–File
The data input to PERMAS is arranged in data blocks, which are enclosed by brackets of
different level. Within a level, the data blocks may be arranged in an arbitrary sequence. The
data blocks representthe basicdatastructure presentedin sections 1.2.1and1.2.2.
The high level brackets $ENTER ... $EXIT enclose data related to a component, as well as
componentindependentdata,likematerialdata. Mediumlevelbrackets$name... $ENDname
enclose data blocks within high level brackets, e.g. variant definitions. The lines to close the
brackets ($EXIT,$END)are always optional. Theinputfile is closed by the delimiterline $FIN.
Theinputstructure is shownin the followingschematicexample:
$ENTER COMPONENT NAME=FRAME
$STRUCTURE
! ............ variant-independent input for current component
$END STRUCTURE
! ... comment sign
$CONSTRAINTS
! ............ input for constraint variant
$END CONSTRAINTS
$SYSTEM
! ............ input for system variant
$END SYSTEM
$LOADING
! ............ input for loading variant
$END LOADING
$RESULTS
! ............ input for result variant
$END RESULTS
$MODIFICATION
! ............ input for modification variant
$END MODIFICATION
$SITUATION
! ............ definition of situation
$END SITUATION
$EXIT COMPONENT

Discussion ofsome ElementTypes
When selecting an element it should be taken into consideration whether it is suitable for the
problem, i.e. whethera modelis capable of covering those points of the reality relevant for the
analysis. These include: shape, restraint conditions, material and load. Below some element
types arepresented:
• MembraneElements
FLA2,TRIM3,QUAM4withlinearshapefunctionsandconstantstressfieldsformodelling
of membranes. In order to obtain accurate stresses with these elements, the mesh must
bemuch finercomparedto a mesh consisting ofhigherorderelements.
FLA3,TRIM6,QUAM8,QUAM9withquadraticresp. biquadraticshapefunctionsformod-
elling of plane stress or plane strain problems with exact representation of linear stress
fields.
• Three–DimensionalElements
TET4, PYRA5, PENTA6, HEXE8 with linear displacement fields and constant represen-
tationofstress field.
TET10,PENTA18,HEXE27withquadratic,biquadraticandtriquadraticdisplacementfield
andrepresentationoflinearstress fields.
PENTA15, HEXE20 with parabolic curved edges,with nodes only on their edges(seren-
dipityelements),notsuitable for contactproblems.
• BeamElements
BEAM2generalbeamwith variable cross-section, optionallywith eccentricity
BECOScentric or eccentric beamwithsolid cross section.
BECOCcentric or eccentric beamwiththin–walled,constantcross section.
BETACcentric oreccentric beamwith thin–walled,taperedcross section.
BECOPcentric or eccentric beamwiththin–walled,openandconstantcross section.
BEAM2W general beam with variable cross-section and warping dof, optionally with ec-
centricity
• PlateandShellElements
QUAD4, TRIA3forthick andthinplatesandshells.
TRIA3Kfor thin platesandshells, with betterbehaviourasTRIA3
QUAD4S,TRIA3Ssandwichshellelements.
SHELL3, SHELL4for thin laminatedplatesandshells.
QUAMS4, TRIMS3for nonlinearanalysis ofthinor thick shells
QUAMS8,QUAMS9, TRIMS6 as higher order elements for nonlinear analysis of thin or
thick shells
• Three–DimensionalGasketElements
GKPNT6, GKHEX8with linear displacementfields and constant representation of stress
field.
• ElementsforSprings,BearingsandSupports
SPRING1linearspring in spacewith single stiffness alongits axis.

LinearMultipointConstraints
Multipoint constraints (see $MPC) can be defined in the structure bracket as well as in the
constraint bracket. PERMASdistinguishesbetweencoupleddegreesoffreedom,rigidregions,
interpolationregions(alsoforvolume–shelltransitions)andgeneralMPCs. Examplesforsome
types ofconstraints areshownbelow.
$MPC SAME DPDOFS = 2
1001 20 : 11 12 13 14 15
The $MPC SAME with identifier 1001 assigns the value at degree of freedom 2 at node 20
to degree of freedom 2 at nodes 11 to 15. Node 20 is the guiding node, nodes 11 to 15 are
dependentnodes.
$MPC JOIN DPDOFS= 1,2,3
1010 GSET : DSET
$MPC JOIN describes pairwise identical displacements. In this example the degrees of free-
dom1,2and3atthedependentnodesinnodesetDSETareforcedtohavethesamevaluesas
degreesof freedom1, 2 and 3 of the correspondingguidingnodesin set GSET. Nodepairs are
determinedaccordingtosmallestdistance. Bothsetsmustcontainthesamenumberofnodes.
Note that both types of MPC above do not take into account the location of the nodes or the
direction ofthe degreesoffreedom($ROTB).

in the nodeset RIGSET are associated with the guiding degrees of freedom of node 20. Any

ContactBoundaryConditions
In contrast to fixed boundary conditions, contact boundary conditions can open or close de-
pendent on the deformation. Penetration of the contact partners is prevented. Definitions of
contactboundaryconditionsmaybe basedon surfaces ornodes.

$CONTACT NODE CONTSYS = 23 AXES = 1
SHAFT2HUB SHAFT : HUB
$CONTACTNODEisdefinedbetweenpairsofnodesandnormallyrequirescompatiblemeshes.
Here contact is specified between node sets SHAFT and HUB. Node pairs are determined ac-
cording to smallest distance. Both sets must contain the same number of nodes. The normal
direction is defined by the first axis of reference system 23, which in this example is the ra-

comparedtoincompatiblesurfacecontact,butrequiresthespecificationofthenormaldirection.

1.4.5 Loading Variant
Oneloadingvariantcontainstheloadingdefinitionsforaspecificanalysis. Eachloadingvariant
may consist of an unlimited number of loading patterns, in other terminology often called load
sets.
Each loading pattern may consist of different loads,e.g. concentrated loads,distributed loads,
prescribedfreedomvaluesorinertialoads. Allloadswiththesameloadingpatternidentifieract
simultaneously. Exampleforanodalforceactinginlocaly-direction(dof2)ofnode5inloading
pattern 4:
$CONLOAD LPAT=4 DOFTYPE=DISP
5 2: 10000.
Dependent on the element type and type of analysis, a multitude of distributed loads is avail-
able, for example pressure loads ($DISLOAD PRESS). Distributed loads may be specified in
differentways:
$DISLOAD: distributed loadsdefinedatelements
$DISLOADN: distributed loadsdefinedatnodes
$DISLOADS: distributed loadsdefinedatsurfaces
Furtherdistributed loadsareavailable,see $LOADING, andthe ElementAtlas.
Alsothepropertiesofcontactboundaryconditions($CONTACTLOAD)aredefinedintheload-
ing variant.

doftype,howeverSIunitsare alwayspresentedin thefirst columnofeach table.

= DISP) that are derived from the basic physical units. For temperature degrees of freedom,
tableT1-9servesasinformationforsomepossibleunitsystems, whereastableT1-11summa-
rizes the information for electromagnetic field computations. The safest choice in any case is
the usageofSI-units,which aregiven in thefirst columnofTableT1-8to T1-11.

1.5 Solution Control (UCI)
1.5 Solution Control (UCI)
PERMAS is controlled by a stream of commands submitted by the User Control Interface
(UCI). These commands may be submitted by one or several files or by interactive terminal
input. Commandfiles maybeincludedup to adepthof10filesusing thecommandINCLUDE.
Whenever an end-of-file mark is reached, control is returned to the next higher include level
(respectivelytheinteractive commandinputaslastpartofthechain). Thedefaultextensionfor
such a controlfile is UCI.
The user control interface has a menu structure and is partitioned into several sections. The
mainsection oftheUCIcontainsbranchesto the different(sub)sections.
Asectionprovidesspecificsectioncommands,whichareavailableonlywithinthisenvironment
(command menu). A section is entered by typing the section name and may be left either by
the RETurn command, by entering a new section name or by terminating the PERMAS run
(STOP).
FigureF1-19givesanoverviewaboutthe availablesections,which are listed below:
STARTUP: Providesthe commandsfor the setupofthe system andthe system start.
INPUT: Controlstheinputofmodeldata.
EXEC: Providesthe commandsto generateprimary andsecondaryresults. Thetime con-
sumingoperationsofthe analysis aremanagedwithin this section.
SELECT: Contains several utility functions, like transformation, summation and further pro-
cessing ofresults.
PRINT: Controlstabularoutputto the results file (RES).
EXPORT: Controlstheoutputof datain variouspostprocessorformats.
USER: Allowsto activate userwritten solutions.
In addition to the section commands and transparent commands, which are available only in
specific sections, thereare also globalcommandswhichare availableeverywhere.
Global Commands
DEFINE, REPORT, RETURN, SET, STOP, TASK ...
STARTUP INPUT EXEC SELECT PRINT EXPORT USER
DEFAULT COMPOSE COMBINE TRANSFORM CURRENT GO CALL APC
MODIFY DOORINFO GENERATE XYDATA ITEM ITEM
NEW READ STATIC SUMMARY MODEL
WEIGHT
Transparent Commands
ACTIVATE, ACTIVE, DISPLAY
FigureF1-19: UCI,Primary Sections
V 19.00.287 PERMASUser’s ReferenceManual(EDU) 1-47
Intro
1 Introduction to PERMAS
Thecommandinterpreterofthe usercontrolinterface works in two modesofoperation:
1. TheDirectMode,wherecommandsareexecuted directly.
2. TheTaskMode,wherethecommandsarequeuedtobecheckedfirstandtobeexecuted
afterwards as a whole. The task mode is invoked and terminated by the global UCI-
command TASK (END). A task is valid for one configuration and the related situations of
amodel. In case ofseveralconfigurations,each configurationrequiresa separatetask.
The task modeis intendedto group commandswith the possibility to check the consistency of
commands and data before the time–consuming execution of the analysis steps begins. This
operation mode helps to avoid errors at an early stage of the execution, saving computer time
andworking hours. Itis mandatoryforall commandsof theEXECsection.
An analysis is executed by a single command, a predefined solution step. As a rule of thumb,
eachsolutionstep isrelatedtoa situationofitsown,whichdefinesthecombinationofvariants
to be analyzed and also provides an environment for the storage of results. On UCI level, the
solution step definesa computationaltask thatin turn invokes a certainsequenceofPERMAS
procedureswhich themselvesactivate allrequiredprocessors andcontrolfunctions.
PERMAS offers standard solutions for a great variety of computationaltasks. Even a complex
task is definedby only a few UCI commands. As an example,a complete static analysis for all
componentsof a configuration (all substructures to be actually treated) is performed using the
UCI-commandSTATIC(to RESIdual):
NEW ! initialize database
INPUT ! input of model
READ PERMAS FILE = model.dat
READ PERMAS FILE = loadsBC.dat
RETURN
!
TASK
EXEC
ACTIVATE SITUATION = S1 ! select a set of BC, loads, properties etc.
STATIC ! perform a linear static analysis
! including displacements and reactions
GENERATE ELEMENT STRESS ! calculate stresses
EXPORT
GO FILE = static_res ! write all results in standard
! postprocessor format
TASK END
STOP ! terminate the analysis
A detailed description of the UCI syntax and of the available commands can be found in the
PERMASUser’s ReferenceManual,chapter2.
ThePERMASExamplesManual(EDU)containselaboratedexamplesforalltypesofanalyses.

1.6 Important Files
1.6.1 PERMAS input files
PERMAS.DFT Definitionofsystem defaults
Is an ASCII file to set up permanent definitions like database file sizes
andlocation.
[project.dat] Modeldescription
is an ASCII file with the model data (e.g. nodes, elements, boundary
conditions).
[project.uci] Solutioncontrol
isanASCIIfile to selectthe typeofanalysis (e.g. linearstatics) aswell
assolutionparametersandoutputrequests.
Extra !#if...!#endif constructs in UCI/DFT/DAT:
The UCI/DFT and DAT syntax rules are described in great detail in UCISyntaxRules and
DataInput(DAT) respectively. Moreoversome extra !#if / !#else / !#endif constructs may
be used inside those input files in order to share them between different PERMAS versions
and/orservers with optionallydifferentfeatures,capabilitiesand/orsettings. E.g.:
!#if (version > 14.10) then
DEFAULT SET VERIFICATION = MODEL
!#else
DEFAULT SET MODEL = VERIFICATION
!#endif
makes use of the VERIFICATION switch available with PERMAS V15 and falls back to the
correspondingMODELswitch in olderPERMASversions. Ora simple feature querybye.g.:
!#ifdef XPU then
! special settings for NVIDIA GPUs (i.e. Tesla K20/K40)
DEFAULT SET PAGESIZE = 2048. ! pagesize 2048 kB
DEFAULT SET NMATP = 4
DEFAULT SET NMATPv = 4
DEFAULT SET NMATP2 = 32
!#if ($PERMAS_XPU_DEVICE == P100-PCIE-16GB) then
! special improved settings for Tesla P100 GPU
DEFAULT SET PAGESIZE = 4096. ! pagesize 4 MiB
DEFAULT SET NMATP = 5
DEFAULT SET NMATPv = 5
DEFAULT SET NMATP2 = 68
!#endif
!#endif
sets anextra largepagesize plussome specialDMSparameterif a XPUacceleratordevice is
used.
V 19.00.287 PERMASUser’s ReferenceManual(EDU) 1-49
Intro
1 Introduction to PERMAS
Currentlythe followingconstructs areavailable:
!#ifdef key [then]
!#if (key cmp value) [then]
!#else ifdef key [then]
!#else if (key cmp value) [then]
!#else
!#endif
With !#elifdef, !#elif & !#fi servingasadditionalshortcutsfor !#else ifdef, !#else if
& !#endif respectively.
Currentlysupported cmp operatorsare: =,==, >,>=, <,<=, <>,/=, !=
For key any system environmentvariable as well as UCI switches or UCI DEFAULTswitches
canbeused(plusthebuilt-inparameter shared, cores, slots,bitspw,thePERMAS version
number and XPU feature as shown in the preceding examples and the (case-insensitive) def-
keys permas and visper to check the current execution type). Environmentvariables may be
marked by $and/orenclosed in braces,asshownin thefollowingexample:
!#if ( HOST == server1) then
define dms dir = /scratch1/
!#else if ($HOST == server2) then
define dms dir = /scratch2/dms/
!#else if (${HOST} == server3) then
define dms dir = "/scratch/%(user)/"
!#endif
Remarks:
1. Thesamemechanism–with#!ifinsteadof!#if(commentstarter#insteadof!)–can
be used in the .permasrc resource file (however, querying a resource variable ahead of
its definitionshouldbeavoidedandmayendin unpredictableresults).
2. Currently all cmp operations are based on simple lexical order, even if an integer/float
value is specified.
3. An additional !-prefix can be used to negate an if condition (e.g. #if !(HOST == hugo)
is identicalto #if (HOST <> hugo)).
4. Keep in mind that earlier PERMAS versions may not support all !#-constructs shown
in this section. Hence – when setting up version aware UCI/DAT files – it might be
necessary to restrict !#-constructs to the former capabilities accordingly (i.e. the base
!#-functionality was introduced with PERMAS V14.00.365, so it won’t work with earlier
versions).
5. Since PERMAS V17.00.210 !#if... constructs may also be nested and/or indented
(this featurewill notwork with earlierversions).

1.6.3 Protocol File
Theprotocolfile containstheechooftheUCI–commandswithextensive informationregarding
all individual steps performed during the analysis, e.g. error messages, diagnostics, list of
procedures,processors(basiccomputationaloperations),dataobjects,anechooftheswitches
andcontrolvariables,statistics aboutcomputationandI/O-time, diskspace andresources.
Startofprotocolfile
Theprotocolstartswithageneralinformationaboutthecurrentprogramversion,thesitewhere
the job wasrunningandsome projectinformation like: project-name,date andstarting time. A
detailedexplanationcan befoundin section 1.6.5.
At program start the standard settings of the PERMAS switches is reported. The switches are
documentedunderthe UCISETcommand.
Thecurrenttime is printed astheleftmost informationin the run protocol.
The protocol file contains an echo of all processed UCI commands. Input and output files are
reportedin addition.

cution. This job is running in parallel with two executor threads (command line option ’-shared
2’).
An estimation of resources is done during constraint module consolidation. It is important for
planing disk space and CPU time requirementsfor big models. This estimation is available as
partofthe task scanningprocess.
A summaryofthe modelcharacteristics is also given.

Statistics for eachprocedurestep
As shown above,for each procedure step (major computationalstep) the following information
is indicated:
• Startof thesolution step
Thesolutionstep nameandpurpose
• Endofthesolution step
The number of I/O Operations between memory and disk, if any, and the used CPU and
elapsedtime. Furthermorea summaryoferrors, warningsandcommentsis given,if any
messageoccurs.
• Within each procedure, basic (arithmetic) operations are performed. These basic opera-
tionsaredonebythesocalledProcessors. Theprocessors(indicatedbyProc)getsome

processors makes the solution process transparent for the experienced user. The ex-

Error messages
Error messagesare issued as soon asproblemsare encounteredduringthe solution process.
If anyerroroccurred duringtheanalysis,anerrorsummaryiswritten attheendoftheprotocol
file:
0 *X* 1 *F* 1 *E* 0 *W*
ERRORS ERRORS ERRORS ERRORS ERRORS ERRORS ERRORS ERRORS
The protocol file should then be examined from top to bottom to find the initial cause of the
problem.
TheErrorSeverity is definedasfollows:
*C* Comment-no programtermination,
intendedforadditionalinformation.
*W* Warning-no programtermination,
hintsto possible errorconditions,should becarefully read.
1-56 PERMASUser’s ReferenceManual(EDU) V19.00.287
ortnI
1.6 Important Files
*E* Error, usually due to wrong or incomplete input data or wrong solution control. The
program continues execution as long as it is meaningful (e.g. to the end of data
consolidation)
*F* Fatalerror- leadingto programtermination
since a continuationis not possible. The reason may be a modelerror or a software
bug.
*X* Internalerror- programtermination.
In most casesa software bughasbeendetected.
Incaseofsyntacticalerrorsinthedata inputfilethecorrespondinglineisechoedintheresult file
togetherwith theerror message.
1.6.4 Log File
If the calculation is made in the background, a LOG file will also be created. It contains the
subset of the protocol file information which is output to the screen, i.e. the echo of the UCI
commandsandpartsoftheprotocolfile alreadyprocessed.

1.6.9 User Stop-File
With a <project>.stop file it is possible to explicitly break a PERMAS iteration (e.g. a con-
tact/NLiterationoroptimizationloop)withoutloosingalreadycomputedresults,i.e. stopfurther
calculations, but export all previously converged solutions. For this the stop-file must contain
the keyword BREAK (with anoptionalcomment)*:
E.g.: myjob.stop
BREAK ! Break all iterations & proceed in UCI (export results so far)
Iftheuserbreaksastatic contactcalculationduringtheiterationofLPAT/TSTEPj,thenallpre-
viously calculated LPATs/TSTEPsup to j-1† will be transformed and exported,i.e. the iteration
stops without error-termination and the rest of the UCI file is executed as if all iterations were
successfull.
Thekeyword KILL directly stopsthe jobwith aPERMASerror terminationandwithoutfurther
exports (butstill closes/deletes the DMS-Filesandgivesa PERMASjob summary,i.e. is more
clean than a simple system ’kill pid’ command). With PAUSE the job can be set to hold and
the keyword TRACE can beusedto print the currentcall-stack withoutstoppingthe job.
Beside the general BREAK command for all running iterations a specific stop request may be
given for a particular calculation step: E.g. STATIC, INERTIA, NLMATERIAL, NLTEMP, NLTIME,
OPTIM, TOPO or VIBRATION will break iterations within the specified UCI command only. More-
over CASOLV, CAU, MLLSOLV, NLEQUI or NLITER will break the corresponding iteration level only
(e.g. maystopthecurrentCA-Iteration,butkeep theaboveNL-Iterationrunningorvice versa).
Additionally a stop file may be used to apply one of the following UCI commands to a running
PERMASjob: DUMP,REPORTorSET (also see additionalremarks onnext page).
keyword invoked action
BREAK Breakalliterationsofcurrent solutionprocedure&proceedin UCI
KILL Kill thejob with cleanPERMASerror termination
STOP Aliasfor BREAK (providedfor backwardcompatibility)
PAUSE Pause thejob (noCPU usageuntilpauserequestis removed)‡ §
PAUSE_LIC Pause andtemporarily free uplicense (e.g. for intermediatetests).¶
TRACE Print thecurrent call-stack (butdon’tstop)
BUCKLING Breakalliterationsofa BUCKlingANalysis
INERTIA Breakalliterationsofan INERTIARELIEFanalysis
NLINERTIA Breakalliterationsofa NLINERTIAanalysis
* Thestop-fileisbasicallyanextraUCIcommandfileandthereforefollowsthesameUCIsyntaxrules.
† Fordebuggingorpost-convergenceanalysisthebrokenLPAT/TSTEPjisexported,too(typicallywithahugetime
offsettomarkthatit’sbroken).Butthisinternal/intermediateresultisnotavalidsimulationresult,ofcourse.
‡ ToremovethePAUSErequestcommentorremovethePAUSEkeywordorjustremovethestopfile.

For’Break’actionsan additionalbreaktime maybespecified, e.g.

will not break the currently running iterations, but will stop a static load history after reaching

Additionalremarkson DUMPandSET:
Keep in mind that changing UCI switch values right in the middle of a running job may cause
an unpredictable runtime behaviour depending on whether or not the underlying solution step
caches the corresponding switch value. Hence – inside a stop-file – only use DUMP or SET
with care. E.g. it is perfectly safe to in- or decrease the job’s verbosity (e.g. SET CAPRINT=4)
butdon’tchangecritical controlparametersofa runningiteration.

1.7 Starting PERMAS
Usually PERMASis startedby the PERMASControlCenter
There may also be site specific solutions provided by the IT department, e.g. in case of batch
queuingsystems.
It is possible to restrict the starting ofthe job on the condition thatall requiredlicense modules
are availablebysetting a! REQUEST.MODULESstatementin the.uci, e.g.
! REQUEST.MODULES = MQA; LS; CAX
If one or more of the requested modules are not available at job starting time (because e.g.
alreadyrequestedby anotheralreadyrunningjob),the job willwaitforthem.
The module names can be found at the end of a .pro file, which may also be generated by a
TASK / TASK STORErun.

Structure of command syntax

∗0

byacolon. onetupleofalistmaycontainitemsofdifferenttypes,buteachtuple
in a list must have the same number of items and corresponding tuples in a list
mustbeofthe same type.

V 19.00.287 PERMASUser’s ReferenceManual(EDU) 2-1
UCI
2 User Control Interface (UCI)
[cont]m conthasto appearbetweenn andm times
n
Braces ( ) contain syntax elements where one element has to be selected. If the selection
{}
is optional, the braces are enclosed by square brackets. The default syntax element, if any, is
underlined.
The command input can be written in free format input lines with a maximum length of 256
characters . One or more blanks serve as separators between different parameters. A com-
mand always ends at the logical end of line. The logical end of line is either defined by the
physical endofline orfrom the commentsign (!) orbythe commandseparator(;).
The comment sign starts documentation text which is of no further relevance. Several com-
mandsmay bewritten onto oneline,using thecommandseparator.
(e.g. HELPNAME=TASK; TASK;EXEC; STATIC; ...).
The logical end of line may be delayed, using the continuation character (&). This allows to
write a command onto several lines. The continuation character must be specified as the last
character onthe commandline.
Some UCI commands allow the input of %-Format Enriched Text (%-Text), i.e. text where the
%-character* allowsthespecificationofsomeself-expandingcontext-sensitiveformatfields,like
e.g. ’the current situation’s name is %(sit)’.
Moreover those % fields may be formatted additionally according to the [s]printf syntax rules,
e.g. SET CASNAME = ’/home/%(user)/%(proj)_T=%12.6(nltime)_with_PERMAS%(vers).cas’.
SeeappendixH for a tableofself-expanding%-fields.
A syntax error in the command input leads to an error message, nevertheless, the command
inputmaybecontinuedin anyway.
* Note,that–inordertopreventanative%frombeingmis-interpretedasaformatspecifier–eachsingle%has
tobemaskedbyadouble%%(exactlylikethe[s]printfsyntaxrules).

2.1 General
Thecommanddescription is partitionedinto thefollowingparts:
1. Syntax description
The syntax description contains all parameters of a command and the sequence of their
specification. If abbreviations are possible, the short form of the command is written in
capitalletters.
2. Parameterdescription
The parameter description explains the possible settings of each parameter of a com-
mand.
3. Remarks (optional)
Containssome hintswhich shouldbewatched,whenapplyingthe command.
4. Description (optional)
If necessary, thecommandisexplainedin moredetailin anextendeddescription.
5. Examples(optional)
Formore complexcommands,an examplemayfollow to illustrate the application.
2.1.2 Important Files
Default file extensions
In order to save some effort in file definitions and to make batch jobs more convenient, some
default filenames are supported. The defaults are connected to the project specification and
differ justin the secondpartofthe filename:
Namingrule : < project > <extension >
The project specification consists of up to 40 characters and serves as the leadingname part.
In the followingtable,the defaultextensionsare compiled.

PERMAS default definition file
The Default Definition File serves to define important parameters for the system startup. It is
an ASCII file which contains commands in free format. It may be modified through editing the
file or in an interactive way through the DEFAULT command. There are several possibilities to
redefinethe defaultsettings. Thesearch rule ofthefiles is as following:
1. Thelocaldefaultdefinitionfile.
Is located in the working directory of the user and is valid for all PERMAS runs in this
2-4 PERMASUser’s ReferenceManual(EDU) V19.00.287
ICU
2.1 General
environment. However, if the changes of some parameters refer just to one project, it is
recommended to use the default command on UCI level instead of a modified version of
the defaultsfile in orderto avoidconfusion forlaterPERMASruns.
2. Thepersonaldefaultdefinitionfile.
It is located in the users home directory and allows to modify the settings due to the
special needs of a certain user. If the changes are not permanent, it is recommended
to use the default command instead of a modified version of the defaults file in order to
avoid confusionfor laterPERMASruns.
3. Thesystem defaultdefinitionfile.
Is located in the PERMAS directory and represents the default settings submitted by
INTES,whichmay beadaptedto reflect generalsettings ofonesite.
Only the first default definition file in the search path is interpreted by PERMAS. The possible
locations of the default definition files are highly machine dependent. Depending on the file
system of the appropriate machine, some locations of the default definition file may be not
existent. Referenceis madeto theinstallation manualsfor adetaileddescription.
Filename Conventions
User defined filenames have to be written in the convention which is valid for the appropriate
machine. Theymaybegivenwiththecompletedirectorypath. Neverthelessthepathdefinition
may be defined separately. Then the final filename is build through a concatenation of the
pathnameandthefilename. Thismaybeadvantageousifseveralfiles arelocatedin thesame
directory.
filnam= [path]fnam
There is nearly no restriction concerning the character set for a filename (i. e. the name
parts). The only character which is not allowed to be a part of the filename is the comment
signwhichalwaysdefinesthelogicalendofline. Afilenamemustalwaysbethelastparameter
of a command, because the end of line mark (or the comment sign) will define the end of the
filename. It may not be continued upon several input lines using the continuation character.
The command separator (;) is also a part of the filename. Therefore it is not possible to write
anothercommandonthe samephysical line.
The user is responsible for the required read / write permissions and the existence of the
specifieddirectories(reading/writing)andfiles(reading). Missingdirectorieswillnotbecreated
by PERMAS.

2 User Control Interface (UCI)
2.1.3 Keys
Thetreatmentof keys is partitionedinto two parts.
1. Globalkeys
2. Localkeys
Global Keys are available within the whole system. They are of interest within (nearly) all
sections. They are treated within a centralized switch handler and may be set/shown through
the globalSET/SHOWcommands.
LocalKeysareofinterestonlywithinaspecialenvironment(oneorafewsectionsareaffected).
Typicalexamplesaresystem initializationparameters. ThesekeysaredefinedinthePERMAS
Default Definition File. They may be changed by the same syntax convention as they are
defined(If they are changeable). Only the default keys which are of interest for the section are
available as parameters of the DEFAULT command of the section. The only exception of this
rule isthe startup section,which knowsalldefaultkeys in orderto initialize the system.
2.1.4 Task Definition
The execution of a task is split into two phases, namely the test phase and the work phase.
During the test phase, all possible tests are performed to ensure that no mandatory input is
missing andthecontrolflow containsnocontradictions. However,nodataobjectsbelongingto
computationalrequests are affected during the test phase. Nevertheless, requests performing
consolidationsteps arealwaysexecuted in orderto beableto do asmuch checks aspossible.
A commandspecified within a task with an erroneoussyntax will notbe introducedin the task.
Therefore it may be corrected immediately without exiting the task (if the definition is done
interactively).
If errors are found during the test phase, the execution of the requests is skipped. The test
phase may also be activated separately. This allows the checking of several tasks one after
another. Since PERMAS allows to examine various variants of a model, the consolidation
process ofthe datais split intotwo phases.
1. Situationindependentdata
They are consolidated once, if the input process is finished. The consolidation is either
invoked through a task definition or by entering specific sections (see chapter 2.5). After
the consolidation process, the last component defined in the input data is active. This
componentisalsothecurrentlyactiveconfiguration. However,nosituationisactiveatall.
2. Situationdependentdata
The consolidation is done as soon as the task is defined which has to be executed for
thechosen situation. Thereforeallvariants ofa modelmay bevalidatedsubsequentlyby
definingandstoring thedesired tasks.
2-6 PERMASUser’s ReferenceManual(EDU) V19.00.287
ICU
2.1 General
Requests coming from Input Doors (e.g. NASTRAN) are translated into PERMAS commands
bythecorrespondingtasktranslators. Theyformseparatetasks,assoonasthetasktranslator
is activated.
Somegeneralrules mustbe obeyedwhendefiningatask.
• The task description has to be initiated in the top component of a configuration, i.e. the
TASK [BEGIN] command must be specified while the top component is active. For sub-
structuremodels,thistopcomponenthastobeselectedexplicitlybeforedefiningthetask.
It is notpossible to changethe configurationaftertheTASK[BEGIN]hasbeeninitiated.
• A task definition requires the successful consolidation of a situation. If there are several
situations, the situation to be examined actually should be activated before defining the
task.
• If no situation is active when entering the task mode (e.g. for default input files) the first
situation definedin themodeldescription will beactivated.
• Material properties which are required for subsequent computational tasks must be
present for all referenced materials of the actual system variant in order to allow an effi-
cient scanningprocessofthe task.
• Formore detailsee page2-55 ff.
2.1.5 Handling of Configurations, Components and Variants
Afterprocessingandconsolidationoftheinputdata,aworkingenvironmenthastobedefinedin
ordertospecifythecomponentstobetreatedbyfollowingcomputationalrequestsandtodefine
the variants ofthe modelto beexamined. This environmenthasto be selected beforedefining
a computationaltask. Thereis a strong hierarchyin activating the computationalenvironment.
1. Activate theconfigurationby specifying the topcomponent
2. Activate thevariants ofthe modelby definingthesituation
3. Activate a special(sub-)componentto restrict someactions to thiscomponent.
Theseactivationsmay bedoneusing the -ACTivate-command(see page2-60).
Nevertheless, if the structure consists of just one component, no configuration has to be se-
lected. If no situation was selected explicitly, the first situation defined in the input data will be
activated bythe system (see task definition,page2-55ff.).
Allcomputationalrequestshandledbythe-EXEC-section (see page2-103ff.) work withinthe
components of the active configuration. The loading, system or constraint variants to be ex-
aminedforthisconfigurationareselectedbytheactivesituationwhichtobedefinedpreviously
throughtheappropriatevariants.

Handlingofvariants
Anarbitrarycombinationofloading,constraintandsystemvariantsofthemodelmaybeexam-
ined by defining the corresponding situations. New situations may be defined at any stage of
thecomputationsandinputdataoftheappropriatevariantsmaybereadinasoftenasneeded,
with the only restriction, that the input of data is no more possible after the successful con-
solidation process of the variant. The exception of this rule are material data which may be
completed (i.e. additional material properties may be added) after the consolidation process
has been performed. However a reference to a new material must be done within another
system variant.
For each of these situations a new (computational) task may be defined. Only the data blocks
andmoduleswhichare subjectto changeswillberebuildforthe differentsituations. Neverthe-
less, each result will be computed only once within one situation. Each of these data modules
is onlyaccessible within thecorrespondingsituation.

of a single variant. The result of any other combination of variants may be derived from these
basic changes.

Parameter Type Value Explanation
BEGIN Optional, indicates the beginning of a task definition. A previous
task definitionmustbeclosed before starting anew one.
END Close the task and start execution due to the task definitions.
Scanningofallcomputationalstepsisincludedbeforestartingthe
execution.
STORE Performallopenconsolidationtasksandscanthedefinedtaskfor
errors
RUN Execute themost recentlySTOREdtask.
LOOPS I 1 Defines the maximum number of task execution loops to be per-
formed. Onlymeaningfulforiterative processes.
Remarks:
1. A task must be invoked in the top component of a configuration. Hence, a configuration
hasto be active beforedefininga task.
2. A task works for an active situation, therefore a situation should be activated previously
(within an active configuration).
3. The -END- or -STORE- option must be given to close the task. If omitted, the execution
will not be performed. In interactive mode, the user is asked for further commands. In
batch mode(UCIfile automaticallyconnected),the run willbe aborted.
4. All time consumingoperations(included in section EXEC)mustbe groupedwithin a task
in orderto dobasic verifications beforestarting the execution ofthosesteps.
Description:
TASK[BEGIN]initiatesthe followingoperations:
• Invokes the inputofdefaultinputsources(if no inputhasbeendoneso far).

result can be processed by postprocessor as element result. If the external design
elementnumberexceedsaspecific number(16777216 on32bitcomputer)internal
designelementnumberingis used.

2.4 The STARTUP section PRESET
Preset standard settings
PRESET TOLBASE= tolbase
Description:
Thecommandinitializes standardsettingsaccording to the choice ofthebase value.
A consistent choicefor the system ofunitsfor allinputdata is still underuser’s responsibility.
Parameter Type Explanation
TOLBASE R Multiplicatorfor initialization oflengthtolerancesettings,see remark 1.
Remarks:
1. Thecommandwillre-initialize the lengthdependentSETparameters
TOLNOD,TOLSYS, MPCDISTOL, MPCOUTTOL,
CADISTOL, CAOUTTOL,CAGEOUPTOL, CATOLSLIP,
PFDISTOL, PFOUTTOL, PTDISTOLandPTOUTTOL
with their default values multiplied by the given tolbase factor. The default values are
documentedwith theSETparametersabove.
For example, tolbase=1.0E-2 will re-initialize TOLNOD to 1.0E-5 (original default:
TOLNOD=0.001), CADISTOLto 0.1 (originaldefault: CADISTOL=10.0),etc.
2. Resetting length dependent tolerances may be useful if a geometrically small model is
discretized in SI units (e.g. ’millimeter sized model in meter units’). In such cases the
original defaults for the above listed tolerance parameters may be too large. Consider
using PRESETTOLBASE=1.0E-3(or1.0E-2)in such cases.
3. If aparticulartolerancesettingshallbechanged,thecorrespondingSETcommandmust
be performedafterthe PRESETcommand.

input file different from the standard input which is defined as <project>.<defext> (machine
dependent),wheredefext is thedefaultfile extension (i.e. myproject.dat).

the input of default files if they are entered. Subsequentlythe consolidation process of data is
invoked. Thefollowingsectionsrequire theexistence ofinputdata:

• PRINT

• SELECT

2-106 PERMASUser’s ReferenceManual(EDU) V19.00.287
ICU
CEXE
2.6 The EXEC section BUCKling ANalysis
Remarks:
1. The geometrical stiffness is computed through the displacement state of a previously
performed computation. This state is selected by using $INSERT VARIANT (see pp.
3-525) within the system variant of the current situation. The geometric stiffness matrix
iscalculatedautomaticallyandmustnotberequestedby$ADDMATRIX.Theappropriate
loadingstate is selected using$ELSTATELOAD.
2. System matrix generation is included in the command request. The command may be
terminated after the system matrix generationusing the -SYSTEM-parameter. A contin-
uationmay bedoneby specifying the -MODES-(andfurtherparameters)lateron.
3. Either the number of modes or a load factor limit must be specified. If both parameters
are present,theminimumnumberofmodesgivenby thetwo parametersare computed.
4. By default the modes are normalized to the unit value for outputpurposes. To outputthe
original(stiffness orthonormalized)modes,setswitch MODENORMoff(see page2-25).
5. The given load scale factor limits are compared with the magnitude of the computed
factors, e.g. specifying SIGN = NEGATIVE FACTOR = 1.0, 3.0 yields load scale factors
between 1.0 and 3.0 .
− −
6. Iftwoloadfactorlimitsaregiven,theydefineaninterval. Allmodeswithloadscalefactors
within thisintervalare computed. Thespecification oftwo factors mustbe combinedwith
SIGN = POSITIVE or SIGN = NEGATIVE. Load scale factor intervals are recommended
for experiencedusers only.
7. TheshiftedalgorithmwhichisenabledbyKSHIFT=AUTOmayyieldmuchbetterconver-
gence. It is therefore recommended to be used especially if many iterations are needed
to reach convergence.
Example:
Please refer to Example BA1 of [um550] on page 6-3 ff. Below a schematic example for the
UCIandtheadditionalinputneededto perform a buckling analysisis presented.
UCI-File
! --------------------------------------------
! Buckling Analysis Example
! --------------------------------------------
!
new
exec
!
! Static Analysis to get displacement state
!
activate situation=static
task

COMBINE 2 User Control Interface (UCI)
Parameter Type Value Explanation
STRAIN/ KINETIC strain orkinetic energydensities.
ENergyDENsity
STRESSRESultants Combineelementstress resultants
TEMPerature Combinenodalpointtemperatures
VELOcity Combinevelocity
BOOK name Nameofanexisting inputbookto becom-
bined.
RESULT name Nameofresult book(see remark6)
NEWPAT ADD Buildresultwithoriginalandnewpatterns.
ONLY Build resultonlywith newpatterns.
Remarks:
1. COMBINE allows to superimpose results referring to loading pattern or time steps by
applicationofpredefinedcombinationrules.
2. The combination rules are defined in the data input using $COMBINE RESULTS (see
page3-1003ff.) within theresult specification bracket.
3. Theresultcombinationis performedfor the active configuration.
4. Ifcombinedresultscontainanyresultsofnon-linearanalysesorofanalyseswithcontacts,
the combined result columns are in general no longer valid results and should be used
onlywithextreme caution.
5. Ifarulereferstoforeignsituations,thesituationsmusthavebeenscanned,eveniftherule
is not used by an UCI command. The use of named result variants is therefore strongly
recommendedto avoidunintendedreference to a rule.
6. In situ operations (omitting the RESULT option) are only allowed, if the rule refers to
the current situation only and the analysis is linear. The following points apply to in situ
operations:
(a) The item DISPlacement may be overwritten as long as no secondary results have
been calculated so far. All derived results (e.g. reaction forces, stresses) will then
becomputedusing the combinedpatterns.
(b) In situ operationson standardresults are onlypossible as long as no derived quan-
tities have been computed from the primary results. Therefore secondary results
cannotbecombinedin situ.
(c) As an exception, element stresses may be combined without using the RESULT
parameter. Then nodal point stresses may be computed afterwards containing the
combinedpatterns(by usingthe GENeratecommand(see page2-152)).
(d) Forin situ operations,NEWPAT = ONLY can notbe applied.
(e) Insitucombinationofnon-linearresultsmaybeenabledbyUCIswitchNLCOMBINE,
butsee remark 4.

Remarks:
1. Theintegrationparametersα(ALPHA,SET/SHOWseepage2-25),β(BETA,SET/SHOW
see page 2-25) and δ (DELTA, SET/SHOW see page 2-35) for the direct integration may
be modified using the SET command (see page 2-25) before starting the analysis. How-
ever,thoseparametersshouldbemodifiedonlywithgreatcare. Ifδischanged,theHilber
Hughes Taylor method is used as integration method instead of the Newmark family of
methods. In this case α and β are modified internally in order to get an unconditional
stable algorithm.
2. When using nonlinear elements, the algorithm is no longer unconditional stable, so the
time step hasto beselected carefully.
3. The XY-data are prepared for the currently active node set, which should be activated
withinthe task modebefore specifying the directintegrationcommand.
4. TheXY-dataare alwaysrelatedto the localcoordinatesystem atthe node.
5. Initialconditionsmay be specified using the $INIVALdefinitionsin orderto continue orto
refinean analysis.
6. Thedefinitionofatime dependentload$TRANSLOADis requiredforthe analysis.

Description:
Thenonlinearanalysisis realizedthroughapiecewiselinearcomputation. Ageneralnonlinear
solutionprocedurewithlinesearchesisusedforthesolution. Ineachloadingstep,aniteration
is performeduntilthe givenconvergencecriterion is satisfied.
Remarks:
1. In nonlinearanalysis,each situation mustbeanalyzedin a separateTASK.
2. Secondary results (including residual and reaction forces) must be computed using the
GENeratecommandwithin the sameTASKasthe DIRECTNLTEMPcommand.
3. An additional selection of result steps may be done in the data input of the variant using
$NLRESULTS. Otherwise only the final solution and the initial values (at TSTART) are
available.
4. If DIRECT NLTEMP, GENerate and EXPORT are performed in a TASK loop, the current
results will be generated and exported for each time step contained in the list given by
$NLRESULTSplusthefinalsolution. Initial values(at TSTART)are notavailable.
5. XY-results may be extracted from the history information using the XYDATA command of
theSELECTsection.
6. If constant temperature modes occur, the analysis is terminated after the calculation of
theconductivitymatrices. FurthermoreasummaryofbookURBMcontainingthesingular
modesisprintedontheresultfile. Thesummarycontainsthenodeshavingtheextremum
valuesas wellasthe summationoverallnodes. Thisinformation mayindicate whethera
localora globaleffect hasbeendetected.
Ifadefaultpostprocessorhasbeendefined,thetopologydata(itemTOPO)togetherwith
the constant temperature modes are written completely in the appropriate format of the
postprocessor. Theretheymay beevaluatedin moredetail.
The default postprocessor may be defined using the DEFAULT command or the setting
maybeincludedin the defaultdefinitionfile.
7. The setting of a minimum time increment is a break-off criterion for the iteration. If the
actual time increment is below the given value, the process is terminated. The criterion

should be applied only with great care, since for a highly nonlinearmaterial behaviour, a

STEPS = LIST is given. In this case the time TEND is equal to the maximum time given

UCI
DIRECT NLTIME 2 User Control Interface (UCI)
Description:
Thenonlinearanalysisis realizedthroughapiecewiselinearcomputation. Ageneralnonlinear
solutionprocedurewithlinesearchesisusedforthesolution. Ineachloadingstep,aniteration
isperformeduntilthegivenconvergencecriterion issatisfied. Themateriallawisintegratedon
elementlevelatthe Gausspointsbyvarioustechniques.
Remarks:
1. Unsupported element types are treated as linear (material and geometry). A table of
supportedelementscan befoundonpage5-16ff. of[um550].
2. In a nonlinearanalysis,each situationmust beanalyzedin a separateTASK.
3. A combination of PLASTIC/VPLASTIC and NLELASTIC material is not supported, even
if assigned to different elements. A table of possible material combinations can be found
onpage5-16ff. of[um550].
4. Secondary results (including residual and reaction forces) must be computed using the
GENeratecommandwithin the sameTASKasthe DIRECTNLTIMEcommand.
5. Secondary results like stresses and strains are calculated at the Gauss points and as-
signed(notextrapolated)to theelementnodes.
6. A selection of result steps may be done in the data input of the result variant using
$NLRESULTS. Otherwise onlythefinalsolution is available.
7. If DIRECT NLTIME, GENerate and EXPORT are performed in a TASK loop, results will
only be generated and exported if the current load step is contained in the list given by
$NLRESULTS.
8. XY-results may be extracted from the history information using the XYDATA command of
theSELECTsection.
9. Initialconditionsmay be specified using the $INIVALdefinitionsin orderto continue orto
refinean analysis.
10. Thedefinitionofatime dependentload$TRANSLOADis requiredforthe analysis.
11. Existing non-symmetric material stiffnesses (non-associative plasticity) are always sym-
metrized.
12. The setting of a minimum time increment TMIN is a break-off criterion for the iteration.
If the actual time increment is below the given value, the process is terminated. The
criterion should be applied only with great care, since for a highly nonlinear material
behaviour,a smalltime step doesnotimply convergence.
13. ThedefaultvalueforTEND=1.0isoverwrittenassoonasaresultvariantusing$NLRESULTS
STEPS = LIST is given. In this case the time TEND is equal to the maximum time given
in theresult variant.

2.6 The EXEC section FSCoupled VIBration [ANalysis]
Description:
Forthe solutionofthe coupledeigenvalueproblem,two methodsare provided.
1. TheMobility-Flexibility (MF)Formulation,
which is obtainedby a force formulation of the eigenvalueproblem,leadingto an inverse
mass (ormobility) andaninverse stiffness.
2. TheStiffness-Mass (SM)Formulation,
which is obtained by replacing the pressure by a suitable kinematic quantity. Hence us-
ing this method, the decomposition of the compressibility and the mobility matrices is
performedinstead ofthedecompositionofthe correspondingdisplacementquantities.
For the reader’s convenience some guidelinesfor deciding whether to use the MF- or the SM-
Formulationshallbesummarized subsequently.
When the coupled system has neither rigid body modes nor constant pressure modes both
methods are equivalent. If the fluid is incompressible and has no surface waves, the SM-
Formulationmightbemoreefficient. SincethecompressibilitymatrixiszeroitsCholeskyfactor
need not be computed and the operations involving it can be skipped. If, on the contrary, the
massofthesolidstructureissosmallcomparedtothemassofthefluidthatitcanbeneglected,
the MF-Formulation is the better method for now the operations involving the Cholesky factor
ofthe massmatrix can beskipped.
Ifthecoupledsystem hasrigidbodymodesbutnoconstantpressuremodesitisbeyonddoubt
that the SM-Formulationshould be used in orderto avoid the problemscaused by the singular
coupling term. For the same reasons the MF-Formulation is the appropriate method when
the coupled system has constant pressure modes but no rigid body modes. Remember that
the MF-Formulation must be used if the coupled system has constant pressure modes and a
vanishingcompressibility matrix.
If the coupled system has both rigid body modes and constant pressure modes, the singular
couplingtermispresentaswellintheMF-FormulationasintheSM-Formulation. Provideditis
notnecessarytousetheMF-Formulationbecauseofazerocompressibilitymatrixthatmethod
should be adopted that allows to approximate the singular coupling term. Should this not be
possibleselecttheMF-Formulationwhenthenumberofunknownsofthefluidissmall,andthe
SM-Formulationifthe numberofunknownsofthesolid structure is small.
Theselection ofthe appropriatemethodisillustrated bytable T2-47.

Generation of secondary results
GENerate(DOFTYPE=DISP)
Remarks:
1. Primaryresults musthave beencomputedpreviously.
2. Generate stresses via the Smooth Patch Recovery method. This method is based on a
least square fit of a polynomial stress ansatz using stresses at a number of supercon-
vergent stress points within a patch of elements. Each patch consists of a corner node
and the connected elements. Hence, SPR stresses can only be determined within ele-
ments with at least one corner node located in the interior of the mesh. SPR stresses
areavailableforthefollowingelementfamilies: flange,membrane,solid,shell,solidshell,
axisymmetric membraneandaxisymmetric solid. Seesection 6.3.1.
3. This generate command must be placed within the same task as the primary command
request to get the full history selected by $NLRESULTS. Otherwise only the last state is
available.
4. Note: GENerate ELement STRESS with ESET option should be put in a separate task.
If a previous command in the same task (e.g. STATIC) creates implicitly elemental dis-
placements,theapplicationofthe elementfilter will affect theseandallderived results.

Description:
The solution calculates the displacements of a free body under static and inertia forces by a
quasi-static solution. As in the standard inertia relief procedure, absolute displacements are
beingcalculated.
Theprocedurecalculatestheinertiaforces correspondingtotheappliedload,i.e. thoseinertia
forces that generate the opposite reaction forces as the applied loads. The inertia forces are
addedtotheappliedloadsandthedisplacementsarecalculatedundertheassumptionthatthe

Parameter Type Value Explanation

onpage2-200).
TSTART R Starting time for analysis, only applicable for contact
analysis with load history. If omitted the minimum time
given by $NLLOAD and/or $NLRESULTS is used, see

$NLRESULTS(or$NLLOAD)is used,see remark6.
Description:
The solution calculates the displacements of a free body under static and inertia forces by a
quasi-static solution. Thisprocedureis knownas’inertia relief’.
Theprocedurecalculatestheinertiaforces correspondingtotheappliedload,i.e. thoseinertia
forces that generate the opposite reaction forces as the applied loads. The inertia forces are
addedto the appliedloadsandthe displacementsare calculated such thattheydo notcontain
anyrigid bodymotions.
Remarks:
1. Themodelmustcontainrigidbodymodes,whichmayeitherbedeterminedautomatically
orexplicitly be specified bythe userwith $RIGMODE.
Thedeprecatedwayofspecification by$EXTERNALis nolongerpossible.
2. Thestaticloadsareappliedasusual,butaloadingvariantisexpectedtobepresentalso
for allsubcomponents,since the analysis createsadditionalloads.
3. The user may define break points through the definition of the end points of the analy-
sis. The break points are given through the command alternatives within the PERMAS
command.
4. Contactanalysis isperformedautomaticallyif contactconditionsaredefined.
5. The static loads are applied as usual. Additional displacement dependentloads may be
introducedwith the $LCMATRIX(see page3-835ff.) statement.
6. If a load history (i.e. $NLLOAD) is given the calculation is performed in the quasi-time
domainfrom TSTARTto TEND, with the defaultvalues:
TSTART= mintime from $NLLOADand/or$NLRESULTS,
TEND = max. time from $NLRESULTSif existing, from $NLLOADotherwise.
Note that the UCI parameter TSTART and TEND can only limit the time range of the
pre-defined load history from $NLLOAD and $NLRESULTS, respectively, i.e. it is not
possible to addnewadditionaltime stepsby thisoption.

7. Thecompleteloadsincludingthe inertiaforces are stored in bookUBLIR.
8. If rigid body modes were specified with $RIGMODE and additional rigid body modes
occur, the analysis is terminated after the calculation of the system and load matrices.
Furthermore a summary of book URBM containing the unspecified rigid body modes is
printedon the resultfile. The summarycontainsthenodeshaving the extreme valuesas
wellas the summationover all nodes. This information may indicate whethera local or a

ofgravitydoesnotmove. Forpartiallysupportedstructures,thecenterofthemovingpart
is keptin place. No $RIGMODEdefinitionis requiredforREFERENCE=CENTER.
If REFERENCE is set to RIGMODE, the displacements are determined such that the
degreesof freedom specified by $RIGMODE are not moving. If no $RIGMODE is given,
thecomputationabortswith anerror.
The deformation only differs by rigid body motions for both settings of REFERENCE.
Thereforesecondaryresults such asstresses areidentical.

• MODALROTATING
maybereferred to in a reliability analysis.

offailure).

• Thereliabilityis determinedwith the desiredcovariance ofsimulation.
• Thenumberofsimulationsfortheactualfailurefunctionexceedsthenumberdefined
byparameterSIMUL.
• Thetotalnumberofsimulationsexceedsthe maximumnumberoftask loops.

damping and stiffness matrices. Exception: Diagonal frequency-dependent Control-6

quenciesanda limited numberofloadcases perexcitation frequency. Theaccuracy can

9. The solution scheme is recommendedfor a large modal basis and only few discrete vis-
cous dampingelements. It is applicableif:
• The viscous damping matrix is constant, symmetric and positive-semidefinite. Ex-
ception: Frequency-dependentsymmetric Control-6elementsare supported.
• Thereare noadditional(symmetric orquadratic)stiffness contributions.
• Elementalstructural dampingis notfrequencydependent.
• Thereisnoviscousdampinginsubcomponents(forMLDRCONF=TOP:Allviscous
dampingelementsmust bein the topcomponent).
• Control elements may have frequency dependent stiffness, structural- or viscous
damping.
Theinversion is performedusing theSherman-Morrison-Woodbury(SMW)formulation.
10. Thesystemoptionallowstopreparecondensationmatricesofacomponentwithexternal
dofsfor a subsequentexport. Condensedloadsare onlypreparedforthe system option.
11. If several dynamic load cases shall be analyzed in the same job, the use of an assembly
situation should be considered for performance reasons. System and result variant must
beidentical,onlytheloadingvariantmaydiffer. See$SITUATIONandexampleDRA3V2.

is used as integration method instead of the newmark family of methods. In this case α
andβ aremodifiedinternallyin orderto getanunconditionalstable algorithm.
4. The xy-data are prepared for the currently active node set, which should be activated
within the task modebeforespecifying the modaltime history command.
5. The xy-data are always related to the component system. The command TRANSFORM
(seepage2-325ff.) inconjunctionwithXYDATA(seepage2-327ff.) canbeusedinorder
to extract results in a localcoordinatesystem.
6. Initialconditionsmaybespecifiedusingthe$INIVALdefinitions(seepage3-832)inorder
to continueor to refinean analysis.
7. Thedefinitionofa timedependentload($TRANSLOAD)is requiredforthe analysis. The
doftype mustmatch the type ofthe relatedload(DISP orPRES).
8. If PRIMRES=REDUCED has been selected, the nodal point results are computed for
all nodes, referred by the active node set or the active element set. Secondary results
for elements are possible, if an element set has been activated previously. Primary and
secondary results in subcomponents are not available. Residuals and reaction forces
may becalculated onlyin single components.
At least one set (node or element set) must be active when applying the -REDUCED-
commandoption.
9. ForRFREQ=EIGFREQthecomputationofequivalentviscousdampingisperformedwith
the eigenfrequencyofeachmode,insteadofa constantreferencefrequency.
10. MODAL FSC TIMEHISTORY supports the following non-linear elements: NLSTIFF, NL-
STIFFR, NLDAMP, NLDAMPR, CONTROL3, CONTROL6 and HYST3. In this case the
desired accuracy maybegiven with theACCURACYparameter.

10. If rigid body modes occur, the analysis is terminated after the calculation of the stiffness

3. The parameter TOLDV may be used as alternative convergence criterion (instead of

designvariablesinthelastiterationisbelowthegivenvalue. Anapplicationareproblems
whichhaveno feasible solution.
4. Switching between DSMETHOD = DIRECT and ADJOINT is only possible for STATIC,
INERTIARELIEF,MODALFREQuencyandTEMPeratureanalyses. Theselectionofthe
mostefficientmethodis also dependenton theavailabledisk space. If a largenumberof
designvariablesisdefined,thedirectmethodmaybelimitedbythefact,thateachdesign
variable will cause a full right hand side. In this case, the adjoint variable method might
help(atcomputingtime costs for a largenumberof constraints).
5. Methodsofthe“AOS”modulemaybeusedalsowithDSMETHOD=NONE.Forgradient
based methods, derivatives will then be calculated by difference quotient, leading to an
extra analysis for eachdesignvariable.
6. Optimizationincludingdesignelementsoftype DBEAD,DFREEandDTOPO(see
$DELEMENT) is notpossible with DSMETHOD= NONE.
7. The ACP method uses a more conservative constraint approximation than e.g. the con-
vex approximation scheme and is recommended for highly nonlinearbehavior. This may
be caused by manufacturing restrictions or also by constraints like frequency response
quantities. It is also quite well suited for very large optimization problems, since it has
out-of-corecapabilities.
8. TheGlobalDomainCentering(GDC)approachlooks for a spherewith maximumdiame-
ter inside the feasible region, not for a single optimal solution point. Use DSMETHOD =
NONEforthis option.
9. The Locally improved Dividing Rectangle (LDR) algorithm is a derivative free method
to detect a global extremum. It is suited for a small number of design variables. Use
DSMETHOD=NONEtosavecomputationtime. Requiresthe“AOS”module. Exhausting
themaximalnumberofloopsis the onlyterminationcriterion for thismethod.
10. TheMultiStart (MS) methoduses local optimizers with several starting points. It requires
the “AOS” module. This method exhausts the maximal number of loops. Termination
of the underlying local optimizers can be controlled by the parameters TOLOBJ and
CSTVIOL. The following specific settings may be changed by UCI command DEFAULT
SET:
• OPTMSUBMETH
• OPTMSEED
11. The Optimality Criteria (OC) method is a derivative free method for nodal pointstresses.
TheusageofDFREEdesignelementsis mandatory,seeexampleOP19.
Besides stress as constraint or objective, further design constraints may be defined if
analyticalderivativesare available.

2.6 The EXEC section OPTIM
12. The convergence of the SCP algorithm may be influenced by UCI command DEFAULT
SET OPTCVXMODE. Often, convex linearization (1) will lead to a smaller number of
iterations,while MMA(0)may beadvantageousfor highernonlinearproblems.
13. TheWedge-constrainedLinearprogramming(WLIN)methodisaderivative freemethod,
use DSMETHOD=NONEto save computationtime. Requiresthe “AOS”module.
14. Theterminationcriteriaforthemethodsofthe“AOS”modulearedifferentfromthedefault
convergencecriteria:
• The global methods have no other criterion than reaching the maximal number of
loops.
• The convergence criterion is not applied, if the algorithm is in some special phase,
e.g. initial sampling or construction of finite differences. The WLIN method has a
samplingphaseduringthe first (designvariables+1) loops.
• All the local methods are Trust Region methods, i.e., they adaptively control the
step size. These methods are designed to guarantee convergence to some point
which maybe a solutionofthe optimizationproblemornot. Thelatter case is called
unsuccessful convergence.
• Successful convergenceis reachedwhen
f(best) f(k) < otol f(best) and
| − | ·| |
(k)
c - c¯ < cviol c¯ , j = 1...m.
j j ·| j |
Note that the current objective function value is compared to the objective value of
thebestknownpointandnotto thevalueofthelastpoint(whichis thedefaultwhen
a non-“AOS”methodisselected).
• Unsuccessful convergenceis reachedwhenever
– the relative step size issmaller thantheparameterTOLDV
– andthe successful convergencecriterion is notsatisfied
– andthealgorithmisnotinsomespecialphase,e.g. initialsamplingorconstruc-
tion offinite differences.
Thedefaultvaluefor “AOS”methodsisTOLDV=1.0E-5.
15. Thefollowingdefaultswitches controltheadvancedoptimization solvers (AOS):
• OPTSUBTOL
• OPTPENAL0
• OPTPENAL1
• OPTRUSTSIZ0andOPTRUSTSIZ1

2.6 The EXEC section RESONANT ANalysis
3. Further parameters for the subspace iteration may be modified using the SET command
(see page2-25)before starting theanalysis. Thoseparametersare:
• ADDVEC
• MAXBOX
• CHEBEXP
However,thoseparametersshouldbemodifiedonlywithgreatcare. Especiallyparameter

• RBMITS

TheymaybemodifiedusingtheSETcommand(see page2-25)beforestarting theanal-

6. The iterative solver is restricted to diagonal conductivity matrices, hence only the diago-
nal mass approach is possible and no MPC-conditionsor substructuring models may be
treated forthe time being.
7. The usage of the iterative solution method may be advantageous especially in case of
good conditioned structures. The saving of disk storage is especially for larger models
considerably,sinceonlyanincompletedecompositionofthestiffnessmatrixisperformed.
8. Rigid body modes are treated different by using the iterative solver. The direct solver
separates the rigid body modes (as far as detected) from elastic modes of the structure,
whereasthe iterative methodcomputesthe rigid bodymodeslike elastic modes.

3. If rigid body modes occur, the analysis is terminated after the calculation of the stiffness
