Short Comment
Inputofa shortcommentononeline
$COMMENT text
Parameter Type Value Explanation
text text Textofshortcommentinquotationmarks.
Remarks:
1. Each $COMMENT line defines exactly one comment which belongs to the current envi-
ronment,i.e. to thecurrent component,variant,data type,materialetc..
2. Commentsby$COMMENTlinesareavailableupto nowforcomponents,variants, situa-
tions,sets,geometricaldatarecords,materials,materialpropertiesandgeneralfunctions.
3. $COMMENT lines may not appear within a $LOOP - $ENDLOOP bracket or within a
logicalline,i.e. betweena physical line andits continuationline.
4. $COMMENT lines with short comment cannot have any continuation lines, they are al-
waysrestricted to onephysical line.
Example:
$COMMENT ’Elements of left wall’

V 19.00.287 PERMASUser’s ReferenceManual(EDU) 3-1443
Misc DAT
$DEFVAR 3 Data Input (DAT)
Remarks:
1. $DEFVARlines may appear anywhere and as often as needed in the data input stream,
butnotwithina$LOOP-$ENDLOOPbracket andnotwithinalogicalline,e.gbetweena
physical lineandits continuationline.
2. Input variables used within a $LOOP - $ENDLOOP bracket must be defined before the
$LOOPstatement.
3. Inputvariableswithfixedintegerindex(e.g. VARNAM(3))maybeused,afteritsdefinition,
anywhere in the current data input stream as constant items but not in the logical input
lineimmediatelyafter its definition.
4. If generation is selected, the variable values of type integer, real or double precision are
generatedaccording to
x(i) = x +(i 1) x S I
− ∗
Fornameandtext values,anintegervalue isgeneratedaccording to
k(i) = k +(i 1) k
S I
− ∗
and appended to the constant name part cpname, i.e. the generated name/text is given
by
name(i) =< cpname>< k(i) >
without blanks etc. between name part and number. In case of text variables, cpname
mustbegiven in quotationmarks.
5. $DEFVARlinesmayhave anynumberofcontinuationlines.
6. If KEEP=NO is specified, input variable definitions by $DEFVAR are valid only for the
current data input stream, including, however, data files added by a $INCLUDE (see
page3-1444ff.)-statement.
7. IfKEEP= AUTOisspecified(default),the$DEFVARdefinitioniskeptgloballikeKEEP=YES
as long as the definition is globally unique. However, if the same name is used in other
$DEFVAR statements with a different definition then KEEP=NO is applied (but identical
duplicatesare still kept globally).
8. IfKEEP=YESisspecified,the$DEFVARdefinitionisglobalandvalidforallsubsequent
PERMASdata andUCI inputstreams. In addition,it may be used in correspondingUCI-
commands by the help of self expanding format strings like ’%(defvar[name])’ (if the
same name is used in other $DEFVARstatements with a different definition an error will
beissued).
9. Gobal $DEFVAR definitions may be included, with identical definition, in all subsequent
PERMASdataandUCIinputstreams.

3.6 Miscellaneous $DEFVAR

! create a list of three names
$DEFVAR COMPNAME TYPE=NAME LIST=SUBCOMPONENT_1_1 SUBCOMPONENT_1_10
& SUBCOMPONENT_2_5

! create a (infinite) list of names and ensure global scope:
! MOD_FREQ_11, MOD_FREQ_12, MOD_FREQ_13,...

$IF 3 Data Input (DAT)
IF Command
Starts anIF ...ENDIF construct.
$IF (A lop B) THEN
Parameter Type Value Explanation
A R/I/name/text First operand,see remark5.
lop Logicaloperator,see remark 7.
B R/I/name/text Secondoperand,see remark 5.
Remarks:
1. A $IFline starts an IF ...ENDIF construct.
2. EachIF ...ENDIF construct mustbeclosed by a $ENDIF line.
3. If the logical expression on the $IF line is false, all input lines between $IF- and $ENDIF
linesareskipped.
4. IF ...ENDIF constructs mustnotbenested.
5. TheoperandsAandB maybe inputvariablesdefinedbya $DEFVAR(see page3-1447
ff.) command or constant values. In any case, the type of the second operand, may be
R, I, name or text, must match the type of the first one. Comparing of single and double
precision valuesis allowed. Constanttext operandsmust begivenin quotes.
6. Outside ofa loop,inputvariables must havea fixed integerindex. Within a loop,the loop
countermaybe anindexexpression,see $DEFVAR(see page3-1447ff.) command.
7. Thepossiblelogicaloperatorsarelisted in thefollowingtable:
< Lesscondition
<= Lessorequalcondition
== Equalcondition
/= Notequalcondition
>= Greaterorequalcondition
> Greatercondition
For name or text operands only equal or not equalconditions are available. Comparison
ofnamesis alwaysdonein uppercaserepresentation.
8. $IF lines cannot have any continuation lines, they are always restricted to one physical
line.

4.1 General
Theelementdescription containsforeach elementfollowingparts:
• Basic informationabouttopology,geometryanddiscretisation.
• Geometricaldata.
• Materialproperties.
• Specific propertiesfor eachavailabledegree-of-freedomtype:
– Degreesoffreedomandspecific description.
– Element-basedresults, e.g. stresses.
– Elementloads.
Someparts of the elementdescription, which are commonfor mostor all elementsofa family,
are placed in the introduction to the element family, e.g. the precise definition of local element
systems orthesummaryofallapplicablematerialinputoptions.

4.2 Flange Elements
4.2 Flange Elements
Overview onAvailableFlangeElements:
FLA2 2NodedStraightFlange(Rod) . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-8
FLA3 3NodedStraightFlange(Rod) . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-15
Theflangeelementsaredisplacementmodelsthatarefullycompatiblewiththemembraneele-
mentsQUAMandTRIM.Theirmainapplicationisthusthemodellingofenforcements(flanges,
stringers, prestressing cables) in membraneshellsandin planestress problems.
Both elements have their cross section centroids aligned along a straight axis z’, on which the
elementsnodesare also located.
Flangeelementscan carry loadsonly alongtheir axis (no bending,torsion, orshear stiffness).
If a more general load-carrying capacity is needed, beam elements must be used instead.
Unless there is sufficient support by adjacent elements or boundary conditions, the flange
elementsmayintroduce redundantdegreesoffreedomthatmustbesuppressed explicitly.
When flange elements are combined with other elements it is important that elements of the
same orderare coupled:
• FLA2 elements are compatible with the edges of HEXE8, PENTA6, PYRA5, QUAD4,
QUAM4,SHEAR4,TET4,TRIA3andTRIM3.
• FLA3 elements are compatible with straight edges of HEXE20, HEXE27, PENTA15,
PENTA18, TET10, QUAM8, QUAM9 and TRIM6 if the inner node of the edge is at mid-
pointposition.
Flange elements may have, according to their nature, only homogeneous isotropic material,
thereforea homogeneousmaterialhasto bedefinedwithTYPE= ISO(default). Theappropri-
ate material property type is GENERAL, but SHELL and PLANE, if existent, are accepted in
addition. Allapplicablematerialinputoptionsforflangeelementsaresummarizedinthefollow-
ing table:

4.3 Membrane Elements
4.3 Membrane Elements
Overview onAvailableMembraneElements:
QUAM4 4NodedQuadrilateralPlaneMembraneElement . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-26
QUAM8 8NodedQuadrilateralPlaneMembraneElement . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-34
QUAM9 9NodedQuadrilateralPlaneMembraneElement . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-43
SHEAR4 4NodedQuadrilateralPlaneShearPanelElement . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-52
TRIM3 3NodedTriangularPlaneMembraneElement . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-57
TRIM6 6NodedTriangularPlaneMembraneElement . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-65
The membraneelementsare displacementmodels that are, straight elementedgesassumed,
fully compatiblewith theflangeelementsFLA.
Membrane elements can carry loads only within their reference plane (no bending). Quadri-
lateral elements are mapped into that plane, therefore corner nodes don’t have to be exactly
coplanar. Whenamoregeneralload-carryingcapacityisneeded,shellelementsmustbeused
instead. Unless there is sufficient support by adjacent elements or boundary conditions, the
membrane elements may introduce redundant degrees of freedom that must be suppressed
explicitly.
When membraneelements are combined with flange elementsit is importantthat elements of
the sameorderarecoupled:
• FLA2elementsare compatiblewiththe edgesofTRIM3andQUAM4.
• FLA3elementsare compatiblewith straight edgesofQUAM8,QUAM9andTRIM6,if the
innernodeofthe edgeis atmidpointposition.
Thelocalelementsystem for triangularelementsis definedasfollows:
1. Thex-axis pointsfrom first to second cornernode.

1. Theelementsystem isdefinedatthecrossing pointofthetwo diagonalsinthereference
planewhich is spannedby the midsidepointsofthe fouredges.

The solid elementscan be classified with respect to their geometry or the order of their shape
functions. In terms ofgeometrythereare fourtypes ofelements:
• TheBrick elementsHEXE8,HEXFO8HEXE20andHEXE27.
• TheWedgeelementsPENTA6,PENTA15andPENTA18.
• TheTetrahedronelementsTET4,andTET10.
• ThePyramid elementPYRA5.
Althoughtetrahedronelementsaresufficienttomeshanygeometry,betterresultsareobtained
when brick elements are used whenever possible, restricting the use of wedges, tetrahedrons
andpyramidsto those partsofthe meshwheretheycannotbeavoided.
In terms oftheirorderofshapefunctions,threetypes ofelementsareidentified:
• Elementswithlinearshapefunctions: HEXE8,HEXFO8,PENTA6,TET4andPYRA5.
• Elementswithincompletequadraticshapefunctions: HEXE20andPENTA15.
• Elementswithquadraticshapefunctions: HEXE27,PENTA18andTET10.
V 19.00.287 PERMASUser’s ReferenceManual(EDU) 4-73

4 Element Atlas
The elementwith the same orderof shape function are fully compatible with each otherwhen-
evertheymatchfacetoface. Whenthefacesdonotmatchcompletely(e.g. whentwotriangles
are matedwith a quadrilateral),the fullkinematiccompatibility is lost.
Allsolidelementscarry3displacementdegreesoffreedompernode. Attimesitmaybephys-
ically meaningful to combine solid elements with other elements (e.g. FLA, TRIM or QUAM),
taking into account that at the connections there may be severe discontinuities resulting in
distorted stress patterns.
For the combination of solid and shell elements a volume shell transition using interpolation
regionsis recommended(see page3-150,3-155or3-163).
For all solid elements, the positive face normal is directed outwards and does not depend on
the sequenceofcorner nodesoftheface.

input type is GENERAL. The material may be isotropic or anisotropic, whereby transversely
isotropic, orthotropic, monoclinic and triclinic or general anisotropic material behavior is avail-
able. Beside GENERAL the material property types PLANE and SHELL, if existent, may be
used in addition for the definition of isotropic material. All applicable material input options for
solid elementsaresummarizedin the followingtable:

General Description:
Second order isoparametric displacement model with incomplete triquadratic dis-
placement field (serendipity element). Not suited for contact analysis, since due to
’serendipity’ interpolation the resulting nodalforces for a constant pressure load on
anelementface are positive atcornernodesbutnegativeatmidside nodes.
Stresses:
Method: CalculatedatGausspoints,extrapolatedto nodes.

Properties for Degree-of-Freedom Type DISP:
Degrees of Freedom:
(u, v, w) ateachnode
General Description:
Secondorderisoparametricdisplacementmodelwithincompletequadratic-biquadratic
displacementfield (serendipity element). Not suited for contact analysis, since due
to ’serendipity’ interpolation the resulting nodal forces for a constant pressure load
onanelementface are positive atcornernodesbutnegativeatmidsidenodes.
Stresses:
Method: CalculatedatGausspoints,extrapolatedto nodes.
Storedin bookSIG.DISP: (σ , σ , σ , σ ,σ , σ ) atall nodes
xx yy zz xy yz zx
Printedelementstresses: (σ , σ , σ , σ ,σ , σ ) atall nodes
xx yy zz xy yz zx
Averagednodalstresses: (σ , σ , σ , σ ,σ , σ ) atall nodes
xx yy zz xy yz zx

by$DISLOADNandpage3-765forgeneraldescriptionofdistributedloadsdefinedatsurfaces

ThebeamelementsBECOS,BECOC,BETAC,BECOPandBETOPare formulatedas equilib-
riummodels,basedonengineeringtheoryofbendingandSt. Venanttorsion. Inaddition,shear
effects in bending (BECOC, BETAC, BETOP) and torsion-bending (BECOP, BETOP) may be
included.
ThebeamelementsBEAM2andBEAM2WareTimoshenkobeamswithSt. Venanttorsionand
sheareffects in bending,BEAM2Wincludingtorsion-bendingin addition.
With the exception of the fluid filled pipe element FSCPIPE2, all beam elements have their
cross section centroidsG alignedalonga straightaxis, andmay haveexcentric nodes,i.e. off-
set vectors from nodeP to the correspondingcentroid G .

4.5 Beam Elements
The beam elements with the exception of FSCPIPE2 have homogeneousmaterial. It may be
isotropic or transversely isotropic, where Young’s modulusis used for bendingand elongation,
and the shear modulus for torsion and shear deformation. The appropriate material property
type is BEAM, but GENERAL, SHELL and PLANE, if existent, are accepted in addition. All
applicablematerialinputoptionsare summarizedin the followingtable:
Available Material Input Options for Beam Elements
Material

4.5 Beam Elements
ElementStresses
The calculation of element stresses is only possible, if information about the geometry of the
beam cross-sections is available, i.e. if standard beam cross sections are used. Only normal
stresses due to elongation and bending are taken into account, shear stresses, e.g. due to
torsional deformation, are completely ignored. For each cross section, normalstresses at four
differentpointsarecalculated,which are shownin the followingpictures:

Definitionofinitialdeformations
The initial elongation δ is positive if the beam is stretched. The initial bending deformations
φ can be interpreted as the initial slopes at the ends of a simply supported beam. They are
positive if produced by a pair of positive bending moments. The initial twist deformation θ is
theinitialrelativeangleoftwist andpositive,ifproducedbyapairofpositivetwisting moments.
Thesignconventionsfortheinitialdeformationsthusareinagreementwiththoseforthestress
resultants.

f
offreedomidentifier8.
General Description:
Circular tube with constant ring cross section, filled with a compressible internal
fluid. Theendsofthe tube may beconnectedto othertubes,closed or open. Equi-
librium model for tension, bending (Timoshenko beam), St.Venant torsion, trans-
verse shear. Longitudinal stresses/strains due to internal pressure are included.
Linearinterpolation for displacement of internal fluid along pipe axis. If the internal
fluid is omitted,the correspondingdegreeoffreedomhasto besuppressed.
The mass of the inner fluid is split up between the translational degree of freedom
of the fluid and the translational degrees of freedom of the structure normal to the
pipe axis. If an outer fluid is present, no degree of freedom is associated with that
fluid, but its mass is added to the translational degrees of freedom of the structure
normalto the pipeaxis.
Stresses:
Noelementstresses available,no contributionto averagednodalstresses.
Stress Resultants:
Method: Direct evaluation of stress resultants, including pressure of inner
fluid,at endcross sections, referring to localelementsystem.

4.6 Shell Elements
For homogeneous shell elements the material data describing elastic behavior are split into
datarelatingin-planestressesandstrainscorrespondingwithtensionandbendingdeformation,
anddatawhichrelatetransverseshearstressesandstrains. Thematerialmaybeisotropic,or-
thotropic or anisotropic (i.e. monoclinic), the appropriate material property type is SHELL for
elastic material data, else PLANE. Since heat conduction perpendicularto the shell reference
planeistakenintoaccount,thematerialforheatconductionmaybetriclinicorgeneralanisotro-
pic in addition,the appropriatematerialpropertytype alwaysbeingGENERAL.Beside SHELL
and PLANE,for isotropic material or scalar properties GENERALmay be used in addition. All
applicable material input options for homogeneous shell elements are summarized in the fol-
lowingtable:

For sandwich shell elements two sets of material data are necessary, one set describing the
behavior of cover plates (skins), and another describing core behavior. Therefore elastic data
aresplitintodatarelatingin-planestressesandstrainscorrespondingwithtensionandbending
deformation, and data which relate core transverse shear stresses and strains. The material
may be isotropic, orthotropic or anisotropic (i.e. monoclinic), the appropriate material property
type is SHELL. Since heat conduction perpendicular to the shell reference plane is taken into
account, the material for heat conduction describes three-dimensional behavior, and may be
isotropic, orthotropic or triclinic (general anisotropic), the appropriate material property type
alwaysbeingGENERAL.Allapplicablematerialinputoptionsforhomogeneousshellelements
are summarizedin the followingtable:

Forshellelementswithlaminatedmaterialtherearetwodifferentpossibilitiestodefinematerial

orientationandreferencetoahomogeneousmaterialhastobeinput,andthepropertiesofthe

Degrees of Freedom:
(u, v, w, ϕ , ϕ , ϕ )ateach node

General Description:
Plane element with bilinear displacement field for membrane, linear bending mo-
mentalongelementedgesandconstanttransverseshearforces. Warpedelements
are handled by transformation into a plane reference configuration. Separation of
membrane and bending stiffness is possible. Suited for thin and thick shell appli-
cations. Artificial (small) stiffness for in-plane rotations. Optionally with rigid lever
armsfrom nodalpointto cornerof elementmiddlesurface.
Twoadditionalformulationsare available. Setting
DEFAULT SET LQUADSHAPE = QUAD4N
yieldsa formulation withmodifiedmembraneandbendingstiffness whereaswith
DEFAULT SET LQUADSHAPE = QUAD4R
a formulation is applied where the in-plane rotations are coupled to the membrane
displacementfield.
Control of Stiffness Calculation
Theparametersepinthegeometricaldatainputallowsforseparationofmembrane
andbendingstiffness:
sep = 0 Completestiffness matrix is calculated(default).
sep = 1 Onlybendingandshearstiffness is calculated.
sep = 2 Onlymembranestiffness is calculated.
The inplane rotations, i.e. the rotations about the normal of the mean plane of the
element,are providedwith asmall artificial stiffness, which is givenby
K = (0.01+c)K
ϕz′ B
whereK isameanbendingstiffnessvalue,andcisaparameterwhichisbydefault
B
equals zero and can be modified by geometrical data input. c = 0.01 means no
−
artificial stiffness.
Since the inplane rotations are fully decoupled from the other element degrees of
freedom, the single, flat element has seven rigid body modes. Furthermore, for
plane shell structures the inplane rotation has to be suppressed explicitly at least
at one nodal point. This is no longer true if the modified formulation ’QUAD4R’ is
selected.

4.6 Shell Elements QUAD4S
Properties for Degree-of-Freedom Type DISP:
Degrees of Freedom:
(u, v, w, ϕ , ϕ , ϕ ) ateachnode
x y z
General Description:
Plane element with bilinear displacement field for membrane, linear bending mo-
ment along element edges and constant transverse shear forces. Cover plates
carry inplane stresses only, core carries only shear. Warped elementsare handled
by transformation into a plane reference configuration. Separation of membrane
and bending stiffness is possible. Suited for thin and thick shell applications. Artifi-
cial(small)stiffnessforinplanerotations. Optionallywithrigidleverarmsfromnodal
pointto cornerofelementmiddlesurface.
Control of Stiffness Calculation
Theparametersep inthegeometricaldatainputallowsforseparationofmembrane
andbendingstiffness:
sep = 0 Completestiffness matrix is calculated(default).
sep = 1 Onlybendingandshearstiffness is calculated.
sep = 2 Onlymembranestiffness is calculated.
The inplane rotations, i.e. the rotations about the normal of the mean plane of the
element,are providedwith a smallartificial stiffness, which is givenby
K = (0.01+c)K
ϕz′ B
whereK isameanbendingstiffnessvalue,andcisaparameterwhichisbydefault
B
equals zero and can be modified by geometrical data input. c = 0.01 means no
−
artificial stiffness.
Since the inplane rotations are fully decoupled from the other element degrees of
freedom, the single, flat element has seven rigid body modes. Furthermore, for
planeshellstructures theinplanerotationhastobesuppressedexplicitly atleastat
onenodalpoint.

K = (0.01+c)K
ϕz′ B

−
artificial stiffness.

onenodalpoint.

4.7 Solid Shell Elements
4.7 Solid Shell Elements
Overview onAvailableSolid ShellElements:
QUAMS4 4NodeQuadrilateralSolidShellElement . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-280
QUAMS8 8NodeQuadrilateralSolidShellElement . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-286
QUAMS9 9NodeQuadrilateralSolidShellElement . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-292
TRIMS3 3NodeTriangularSolidShellElement . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-298
TRIMS6 6NodeTriangularSolidShellElement . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-304
The solid shell elements can be classified with respect to their geometry and order of their
shapefunctions. In terms ofgeometrythereare two typesofelements:
• ThequadrilateralelementsQUAMS4,QUAMS8andQUAMS9.
• ThetriangularelementsTRIMS3,TRIMS6.
In terms oftheirorderofshapefunctions,threetypes ofelementsareidentified:
• Elementswithlinearshapefunctions: QUAMS4,TRIMS3.
• Elementswithincompletequadraticshapefunctions: QUAMS8.
• Elementswithquadraticshapefunctions: QUAMS9,TRIMS6.
The elementwith the same orderof shape function are fully compatible with each otherwhen-
evertheymatchfacetoface. Whenthefacesdonotmatchcompletely(e.g. whentwotriangles
are matedwitha quadrilateral),thefull kinematiccompatibilityis lost.
All solid shell elements carry 7 degree of freedoms per node. Linear solid shell elements can
becombinedwith thelinearshellelementsTRIA3andQUAD4.
For the combination of solid and shell elements a volume shell transition using interpolation
regionsis recommended(see page3-150,3-155or3-163).
Lower and upper surface of solid shell elements are defined by the shell director which points
from the lower to the upper element surface. The shell director forms a right hand system
with the axes of the reference surface in the initial configuration at the nodal points. The shell
director varies over and is not necessarily perpendicular to the axes of the reference surface.
Whencommonshelldirectorsatthenodalpointsareused(DEFAULTSETCSHDIR=ON),the
shell directors of adjacent solid shell elements should have approximately the same direction.
Theallowablekink angleis specified byDEFAULTSETCSHDIRKINK.

4.7 Solid Shell Elements QUAMS8
Properties for Degree-of-Freedom Type DISP:
Degrees of Freedom:
(u, v, w, ϕ , ϕ , ϕ , ∆t)ateachnode
x y z
General Description:
Generalshellelementwithcurvededges,incompletebiquadraticdisplacementfield
on reference surface and linear displacement field across the thickness. Suited for
thin andthick shell applications. Artificial (small) stiffness for inplanerotations.
Control of Stiffness Calculation
The inplane rotations, i.e. the rotations about the normal of the mean plane of the
element,are providedwith a smallartificial stiffness, which is givenby
K = (0.001+c)K
ϕz′ rot
where K is a mean rotational stiffness value, and c is a parameter which is by
rot
default equal zero and can be modified by geometrical data input. c = 0.001
−
meansno artificial stiffness.
Since the inplane rotations are fully decoupled from the other element degrees of
freedom, the single, flat element has seven rigid body modes. Furthermore, for
planeshellstructures theinplanerotationhastobesuppressedexplicitly atleastat
onenodalpoint.
Stresses:
Method: Calculated at Gauss points of reference surface and at Lobatto
pointsthroughthe thickness. Extrapolatedto cornernodes.
Storedin bookSIG.DISP: (σ ,σ ,σ ,σ , σ , σ )

atallnodeswith five layers throughthe thickness
first layerbelongsto uppersurface
third layer belongsto the reference surface
fifth layerbelongsto lowersurface

xx yy zz xy yz zx
atallnodeswith five layers throughthe thickness
first layerbelongsto uppersurface

fifth layerbelongsto lowersurface

4.7 Solid Shell Elements TRIMS6
Properties for Degree-of-Freedom Type DISP:
Degrees of Freedom:
(u, v, w, ϕ , ϕ , ϕ , ∆t)ateachnode
x y z
General Description:
Element with curved edges, quadratic displacement field on reference surface and
linear across the thickness. Suited for thin and thick shell applications. Artificial
(small) stiffness for inplanerotations.
Control of Stiffness Calculation
The inplane rotations, i.e. the rotations about the normal of the mean plane of the
element,are providedwith a smallartificial stiffness, which is givenby
K = (0.001+c)K
ϕz′ rot
where K is a mean rotational stiffness value, and c is a parameter which is by
rot
default equal zero and can be modified by geometrical data input. c = 0.001
−
meansno artificial stiffness.
Since the inplane rotations are fully decoupled from the other element degrees of
freedom, the single, flat element has seven rigid body modes. Furthermore, for
planeshellstructures theinplanerotationhastobesuppressedexplicitly atleastat
onenodalpoint.
Stresses:
Method: Calculated at Gauss points of reference surface and at Lobatto
pointsthroughthe thickness. Extrapolatedto cornernodes.

4.8 Gasket Elements
4.8 Gasket Elements
Overview onAvailableThree–DimensionalGasketElements:
GKHEX8 8NodedSolidHexahedron . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-316
GKHEX20 20NodedSolidHexahedron . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-322
GKHEX27 27NodedSolidHexahedron . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-328
GKPNT6 6NodedSolidPentahedron . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-334
GKPNT15 15NodedSolidPentahedron . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-340
GKPNT18 18NodedSolidPentahedron . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-346
Three–dimensional Gasket Elements are used to model sealing components between struc-
tural components. The through–the–thickness behavior is uncoupled from membrane and
transverse shear behavior and is defined by a non–linear pressure/closure curve known from
testdata. Thenonlinearitycanbeelasticorplastic. Membraneandtransverseshearbehaviour
is linearelastic. Thereis no thermalexpansionin through–the–thicknessdirection.
With the default settings (GSKSOLV = CONTACT) the gasket model corresponds to a mem-
branewith decouplednon-linearsprings.
γ
Schematicofa gasketelement
The midsurface behaveslike a membrane element with material parameters E and ν. Decou-
pled springs act in through-the-thickness direction at element edges with a nonlinear gasket
loading curve. The shear behavior of the springs corresponds to a shear modulus G with
τ = Gtanγ.
Element specific results are GASKETCLOSURE and GASKETPRESSURE, which are cre-
atedautomatically.
V 19.00.287 PERMASUser’s ReferenceManual(EDU) 4-311
Elements
Gasket
4 Element Atlas
TheGasketelementscanbeclassifiedwithrespecttotheirgeometryortheorderoftheirshape
functions. In terms ofgeometrythere aretwo types ofelements:
• TheBrick elementsGKHEX8, GKHEX20andGKHEX27
• TheWedgeelementsGKPNT6,GKPNT15andGKPNT18.
In terms oftheirorderofshapefunctions,threetypes ofelementsare identified:
• Elementswith linearshapefunctions: GKHEX8andGKPNT6.
• Elementswith incompletequadraticshapefunctions: GKHEX20andGKPNT15.
• Elementswith quadraticshapefunctions: GKHEX27andGKPNT18.
Elementswith thesame orderofshapefunction arefully compatiblewitheach otherwhenever
they match face to face. Whenthe faces do notmatch completely(e.g. whentwo trianglesare
matedwith a quadrilateral),the fullkinematic compatibilityis lost.
All Gasketelementscarry 3 displacementdegreesoffreedompernode.
By default the through–the–thickness direction of the Gasket elements is orthogonal to the
midsurface between element faces 1 and 6 for the brick elements and element faces 1 and 5
forthewedgeelements. Forbrickelementsalsoanothermidsurfacecanbechosenbydefining
an element system $ELSYS (see page 3-97 and remark 3) in the structure bracket. Then the
through–the–thicknessis orthogonalto the midsurface which is orthogonalto the z’ axis ofthe
elementsystem.
ForallGasketelements,thepositivefacenormalisdirectedoutwardsanddoesnotdependon
the sequenceofcorner nodesoftheface.

4.8 Gasket Elements
Gasket elements have transversely isotropic gasket material. The appropriate material in-
put type is GENERAL. Gasket elements have non–linear material behaviour in through–the–
thickness direction described by $GSKLOAD (see 3-1372) and $GSKUNLOAD (see 3-1377),
respectively. All applicable material input options for gasket elements are summarized in the
followingtable:

4.9 Spring Elements
Stress ResultantsandInitialDeformations
For spring elements only stress resultants instead of stresses are available. They are calcu-
lated for both nodes, referring to the local element coordinate system (x y z ), and can be
′ ′ ′
easily interpreted as the forces acting on the element in order to produce the elastic deforma-

initialdeformations. ForSPRING1,SPRING3,NLSTIFFandNLSTIFFRelementscorrespond-

All available damper elements have viscous damping, i.e. their element forces depend on the
time derivative of the element deformations. Element structural damping, however, may be
representedusing anytype of linear’stiffness’ elementwith materialproperty$DAMPING.

4.12 Viscoelastic Solid Elements
4.12 Viscoelastic Solid Elements
Overview onAvailableViscoelastic SolidElements:
HEXVE8 8NodedViscoelastic SolidHexahedron . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-444
HEXVR8 8NodedViscoelastic SolidHexahedron . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-448
Viscoelastic elements represent a Maxwell model, i.e. elastic and viscous part in series. The
submatricesoftheelasticpartareidenticaltothematricesofthecorrespondingsolidelements,
i.e. for the HEXVE8 element the matrices of the HEXE8 element etc.. To achieve a general-
izedMaxwellorBiotmodel,oneormoreviscoelasticsolidelementsareaddedtoonestandard
(basic) solid element, forming a so-called Prony series. The standard translational degrees of
freedom of all those viscoelastic elements belonging to one basic element must be coupled,
either by identical element node lists (HEXVR8 elements) or coupled by MPCs (HEXVE8 ele-
ments). Thenon-standarddegreesoffreedomofHEXVE8elements,representingtheviscous
part,remainuncoupled.
For all viscous solid elements, the positive face normal is directed outwards and does not
dependonthe sequenceofcornernodesofthe face.

4.13 Load Carrying Membrane Elements
4.13 Load Carrying Membrane Elements
Overview onAvailableLoadCarryingMembraneElements:
LOADA4 4NodeQuadrilateralLoadCarrying MembraneElement . . . . . . . . . 4-457
LOADA8 8NodeQuadrilateralLoadCarrying MembraneElement . . . . . . . . . 4-460
LOADA9 9NodeQuadrilateralLoadCarrying MembraneElement . . . . . . . . . 4-463
LOADA3 3NodeTriangularLoadCarrying MembraneElement . . . . . . . . . . . 4-466
LOADA6 6NodeTriangularLoadCarrying MembraneElement . . . . . . . . . . . 4-469
The load carrying membrane elements can be classified with respect to their geometry and
orderoftheirshapefunctions. In termsof geometrythere are twotypes ofelements:
• TheQuadrilateralelementsLOADA4,LOADA8andLOADA9.
• TheTriangularelementsLOADA3,LOADA6.
In terms oftheirorderofshapefunctions,threetypes ofelementsareidentified:
• Elementswithlinearshapefunctions: LOADA3,LOADA4.
• Elementswithincompletequadraticshapefunctions: LOADA8.
• Elementswithquadraticshapefunctions: LOADA6,LOADA9.
The elementwith the same orderof shape function are fully compatible with each otherwhen-
evertheymatchfacetoface. Whenthefacesdonotmatchcompletely(e.g. whentwotriangles
are matedwitha quadrilateral),thefull kinematiccompatibilityis lost.
Allloadcarrying membraneelementshavethreedegreeoffreedomspernode. Theyareused
solely for the definition of surface loads which act on solid elements. In addition they are able
to calculate the stresses on the boundaryof solid elements, plain stress conditions assumed.
Hence evaluation of stresses on surfaces loaded by out-of-plane loads will give wrong results,
since the effect of stresses normalto the surface is ignored. In any case the material property
of the elements must be identical to the underlying solid elements. They do not contribute to
stiffness, dampingormassmatrix.
• LOADA3elementsare compatiblewiththe surfaces ofTET4,PYRA5andPENTA6.
• LOADA4elementsare compatiblewiththe surfaces ofPYRA5,PENTA6andHEXE8.
• LOADA6elementsare compatiblewiththe surfaces ofTET10,PENTA15andPENTA18.
• LOADA8elementsare compatiblewiththe surfaces ofPENTA15andHEXE20.
• LOADA9elementsare compatiblewiththe surfaces ofHEXE27.

encefrequencyis specified by thecommand.
• Fortimehistoryanalysis,thereferencefrequencymustbeinputinthealignedresult

If, however, the solution procedure performs a loop over rotational speeds (e.g. MODAL
ROTATING(see page2-231ff.)), thenthe actualrotationalspeedis used instead.

Properties for Degree-of-Freedom Type DISP:
Degrees of Freedom:
(u, v, w) ateachnode
General Description:
Discreteequilibriummodelwiththreetranslationalstiffnessesindirectionofelement
axes. No stiffness with respectto rotations.
Theelementisintendedtoovercomestaticrigid bodymodesthatwillbesupported
by later contact forces. I.e. the CA1ZERF3 stiffnesses help to avoid singularities
duringthedecompositionofthestiffnessmatrix,butisnotasupportbyitself–ifthe
correspondingmotionisnotsupportedbyadequatecontactforcestheunsupported
rigid body mode will still result in an infinite movement ! For more details on the
theorywe referto section 4.1.10of[um550].
Stresses:
Noelementstresses available,no contributionto averagednodalstresses.

correction force)at node,referring to local elementsystem.

4.15 Special CA Elements CA2ZERF1
Properties for Degree-of-Freedom Type DISP:
Degrees of Freedom:
(u, v, w) ateachnode
General Description:
Discrete equilibrium model with translational stiffness in direction of element axis.
No stiffness withrespect to transverse displacementsorrotations.
Theelementisintendedto overcomestatic rigid bodymodesthatwillbesupported
by later contact forces. I.e. the CA2ZERF1 stiffness helps to avoid singularities
duringthedecompositionofthestiffnessmatrix,butisnotasupportbyitself–ifthe
correspondingmotionisnotsupportedbyadequatecontactforcestheunsupported
rigid body mode will still result in an infinite movement ! For more details on the
theorywe referto section 4.1.10of[um550].
Unless thereis sufficient supportbyadjacentelementsorboundaryconditions,the
element may introduce redundant degrees of freedom that must be suppressed
explicitly.
Stresses:
No elementstresses available,nocontribution to averagednodalstresses.
Stress Resultants:
Method: Direct evaluation of element forces (force resulting from constant
stiffness k pluscorrection force RCA resultingfromcontactanal-
11 11
ysis) atnodes,referring to local elementsystem.
Storedin bookRSFR.DISP: (N , 0, 0) atbothelementnodes
x
′
Printedstress resultants: (N , 0, 0) atbothelementnodes
x
′

No distributed loadsavailable.

4.17 Line Convection Elements
4.17 Line Convection Elements
Overview onAvailableLine ConvectionElements:
CONAL2 2NodedStraightEdgeConvectionElement . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-554
CONAL3 3NodedCurvedEdgeConvectionElement . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-559
CONL2 2NodedStraightLineConvectionElement . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-564
CONL3 3NodedCurvedLineConvectionElement . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-569
Line convection elements are used to include convective heat transfer at the edges of mem-
branes and shells (edge convection) or along rods and beams (line convection) in thermal
analysis. In addition,theheatcapacity ofthe convective film maybetaken into account.
Line convection elements are restricted to thermal analysis, and are ignored in any other kind
ofanalysis.
If the heat capacity of the convective film should be taken into account, a homogeneous
isotropicmaterialhastobedefinedwithTYPE=ISO (default)andmaterialpropertytypeGEN-
ERAL.Allapplicablematerialinputoptionsforlineconvection elementsaresummarizedin the
followingtable:

4.18 Surface Convection and Radiation Elements
4.18 Surface Convection and Radiation Elements
Overview onAvailableSurface ConvectionandRadiationElements:
CONA3 3NodedTriangularSurface ConvectionandRadiationElement . . . . . 4-577
CONA4 4NodedQuadrilateralSurfaceConvectionandRadiationElement . . . . 4-582
CONA6 6NodedTriangularSurface ConvectionandRadiationElement . . . . . 4-587
CONA8 8NodedQuadrilateralSurfaceConvectionandRadiationElement . . . . 4-592
CONA9 9NodedQuadrilateralSurfaceConvectionandRadiationElement . . . . 4-597
CONS3 3NodedTriangularShellSurface ConvectionandRadiationElement . . 4-602
CONS4 4NodedQuadrilateralShellSurface ConvectionandRadiationElement. 4-607
CONS6 6NodedTriangularShellSurface ConvectionandRadiationElement . . 4-612
CONS8 8NodedQuadrilateralShellSurface ConvectionandRadiationElement. 4-617
CONS9 9NodedQuadrilateralShellSurface ConvectionandRadiationElement. 4-622
Surface convection and radiation elements are used to include radiation and convective heat
transferatthesurfacesofmembranes,shellsandsolidsinthermalanalysis. Especiallyforshell
elements,shellsurfaceconvectionandradiationelementsareavailablewhichtakeintoaccount
the temperature difference between upper and lower surface of the element. In addition, the
heatcapacity ofthe convective film maybetaken into account.
Surface convection and radiation elements are restricted to thermal analysis, and are ignored
in anyotherkind ofanalysis.

FLTET10 10NodedFluidTetrahedron . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-655
The fluid elements can be classified with respect to their geometry or the order of their shape
functions. In terms ofgeometrythereare fourtypes ofelements:
• TheBrick elementsFLHEX8,FLHEX20andFLHEX27
• TheWedgeelementsFLPENT6,FLPENT15andFLPENT18.
• TheTetrahedronelementsFLTET4,andFLTET10.
• ThePyramid elementFLPYR5
Althoughtetrahedronelementsaresufficienttomeshanygeometry,betterresultsareobtained
when brick elements are used whenever possible, restricting the use of wedges, tetrahedrons
andpyramidsto those partsofthe meshwheretheycannotbeavoided.
In terms oftheirorderofshapefunctions,threetypes ofelementsareidentified:
• Elementswithlinearshapefunctions: FLHEX8,FLPENT6,FLTET4andFLPYR5.
• Elementswithincompletequadraticshapefunctions: FLHEX20andFLPENT15.
• Elementswithquadraticshapefunctions: FLHEX27,FLPENT18andFLTET10.

4.20 Fluid Structure Interface Elements
4.20 Fluid Structure Interface Elements
Overview onAvailableFluid Structure Interface Elements:
FSINTA3 3NodedTriangularFluid Structure Interface Element . . . . . . . . . . . 4-661
FSINTA4 4NodedQuadrilateralFluidStructure Interface Element . . . . . . . . . 4-664
FSINTA6 6NodedTriangularFluid Structure Interface Element . . . . . . . . . . . 4-667
FSINTA8 8NodedQuadrilateralFluidStructure Interface Element . . . . . . . . . 4-670
FSINTA9 9NodedQuadrilateralFluidStructure Interface Element . . . . . . . . . 4-673
The fluid structure interface elements are used to couple solid and fluid domains for coupled
analysis. In addition,theymaybeused to includeboundaryabsorptionin thefluid domain.
Each node carries three displacement degrees of freedom and one pressure degree of free-
dom. For a pure fluid analysis without structure the displacement degrees of freedom are
ignored,fora purestructural analysis theinterface elementsare ignoredatall.
If two fluid regions are separated by a thin wall idealized by shell elements (doubly wetted
surface), the problem arises that for one shell node with one set of displacement degrees of
freedom there are two different pressure values, one for each fluid region. Therefore for each
fluid region oneinterface elementis necessary, the first one with the same nodalpoints as the
corresponding shell element, and the second one with different nodes at the same position in
space andthedisplacementdegreesoffreedomjoinedbymultipointconstraints.
The orientation of interface elements must be such that the element normal points from the
fluid to the solid.
Thelocalelementsystem for triangularelementsis definedasfollows:
1. Thex-axis pointsfrom first to second cornernode.
′
2. They -axis isnormalto the x-axis, pointingto thethird cornernode.
′ ′
3. Theelementnormalforms a right handsystem with the x- andy -axis.
′ ′
Forquadrilateralelementsthe localelementsystem isdefinedin the followingway:
1. Theelementsystem isdefinedatthecrossing pointofthetwo diagonalsinthereference
planewhich is spannedby the midsidepointsofthe fouredges.
2. The x-axis lies in the reference surface bisecting the angle between the diagonals and
′
pointing towards the second edge (from the second to the third corner node). For a
rectangular shape the x-axis is parallel to the first edge (from the first to the second
′
corner node).

4.21 Surface Wave Elements
4.21 Surface Wave Elements
Overview onAvailableSurface Wave Elements:
FLWAVEA3 3NodedTriangularSurface Wave Element . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-679
FLWAVEA4 4NodedQuadrilateralSurfaceWave Element . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-682
FLWAVEA6 6NodedTriangularSurface Wave Element . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-685
FLWAVEA8 8NodedQuadrilateralSurfaceWave Element . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-688
FLWAVEA9 9NodedQuadrilateralSurfaceWave Element . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-691
The surface wave elements are used to idealize free surfaces of the fluid where the pressure
atthe surface is balancedby the weightofsurface waves.
Surface waveelementscarry onepressure degreeoffreedom.
Surface wave elements are always placed on the boundary of the fluid perpendicular to the
direction of gravity acceleration. The orientation of the element normal is meaningless. The
gravity acceleration value itself must be inputted by parameter GFLWAVE within the system
variant, seedatablock $PARAMETER,page3-549.
Thelocalelementsystem for triangularelementsis definedasfollows:
1. Thex-axis pointsfrom first to second cornernode.
′
2. They -axis isnormalto the x-axis, pointingto thethird cornernode.
′ ′
3. Theelementnormalforms a right handsystem with the x- andy -axis.
′ ′
Forquadrilateralelementsthe localelementsystem isdefinedin the followingway:
1. Theelementsystem isdefinedatthecrossing pointofthetwo diagonalsinthereference
planewhich is spannedby the midsidepointsofthe fouredges.
2. The x-axis lies in the reference surface bisecting the angle between the diagonals and
′
pointing towards the second edge (from the second to the third corner node). For a
rectangular shape the x-axis is parallel to the first edge (from the first to the second
′
corner node).
3. They -axisliesalsointhereferencesurfacebisectingthecomplementaryanglebetween
′
the diagonals and pointing towards the third edge (from third to last corner node). For a
rectangularshapethe y -axis is parallelto thesecond edge.
′
4. The elementnormalforms a right hand system with the x-and y -axis, i.e. it is normal to
′ ′
the reference surface.

4.23 Two–Dimensional Infinite Elements
4.23 Two–Dimensional Infinite Elements
Overview onAvailableTwo-DimensionalInfinite Elements:
INFFLA2 2NodedStraightInfinite MembraneElement . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-701
INFFLA3 3NodedCurvedInfinite MembraneElement . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-704
INF2QAM4 4NodedStraightInfinite MembraneElement . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-707
INF2QAM8 8NodedCurvedInfinite MembraneElement . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-710
INF2QAM9 9NodedCurvedInfinite MembraneElement . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-713
The Infinite Elementsare special elementsto modelthe unboundeddomain. Yet they are only
availableforelectromagneticandacoustic/fluidproblems. Payattentiontothefollowingfeatures
(see also theoreticalmanual):
• Thefirstpartofthename’INF’indicatestheelementasanINFINITEelement,thesecond
part ’FLA2’ names the element, which is used as the modeling element (here a FLA2
element).
• The geometry of the Infinite Elements tends to infinity and is described with singular
functions.
• ThegeometryoftheInfinite Elementswillbechangedthroughtheprogramanddepends
on theposition ofthe pole.
• Thenodesatinfinityarenotmodeledsincetheyarethoughttobesuppressed(”automatic
Dirichlet boundarycondition”),buttheyhaveinfluence onthe interpolation–functions.
• The degrees of freedom (e. g. potential) are interpolated with the standard functions, e.
g. INFFLA2 with the QUAM4 interpolation–functions without the ones, which belong to
the nodeslying atinfinity.
• The material is always isotropic and homogeneous. No local element system is neces-
sary.
• Thegeometricaldatasare alwaysvalid forall nodes.
• Rotatedbasisis notallowed.
• Theuserhastochoose anexpansionpolewhich isalwaysoppositeto theinfinity side of
the element.
• All Infinite Elementscan carry onlynodalpointloads($CONLOAD).
• Because the infinite elements are modeled with iso–parametric elements, higher order
infinite elements must have their greatest geometrical extension after the modeling in
infinite direction, otherwise they can not be recognized as an infinite element in the right
manner.
V 19.00.287 PERMASUser’s ReferenceManual(EDU) 4-699
Elements
2D-Infinite
4 Element Atlas
• Infinite elements are suitable for static and first order time–changing problems. For the
secondordertime–changingwaveequationaddedmassproblemscanbetreated. Infinite
elements can not handle the full wave equation in the unbounded domain. For those
problemsabsorbingboundaryconditionelementsmust beused.
Infinite elements have isotropic fluid material to emphasize their property of modelling the un-
bounded domain. All applicable material input options for infinite elements are summarized in
the followingtable:

(see also theoreticalmanual)explainedonpage4-699.

modelling the unbounded domain, and the appropriate material input type is GENERAL. All
applicablematerialinputoptionsfor infinite elementsare summarizedin the followingtable:

4.25 Three–Dimensional Bayliss–Turkel RBC Elements
Overview onAvailableThree–DimensionalBayliss-Turkel RBCElements:
RBCBT1A3 3NodedTriangularElementwith StraightEdges. . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-767
RBCBT1A6 6NodedTriangularElementwith CurvedEdges. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-771

RBCBT2A9 9NodedQuadrilatralElementwith CurvedEdges. . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-803
TheRBC(radiationboundarycondition)elementsarespecialelementstoconstructanartificial
boundaryandtoimposeconditionsonthissurfacetosimulateaninfinitedomain. TheBayliss–
Turkel RBC elements are based on the mode annihilating approximation technique. The idea
istoabsorbthemodesofthefarfieldexpansionofoutgoingpropagatingsolutionto the(wave)
equation (the Sommerfeld condition annihilates the first mode of plane waves). For further
details of the theory see (††) (‡‡). The RBC elements of first order annihilate the first mode
of the far field expansion, the elements of second order the first two modes. In general the
elementsofsecond orderare moreaccurate thanthose offirst order.
The theory of Bayliss–Turkel in three dimensions is based on a far field solution in a spherical
coordinatesystem. ThustheRBCelementsmustbeplacedontothesurfaceofaFiniteElement
meshwhichisofsphericalshapeonly. WiththeRBCelementstheinfluenceoftheunbounded
domain is taken into account and the problem is well posed too. So no additional boundary
conditionsforthe unboundeddomainare necessary.
†† A.Bayliss,E.Turkel: Radiationboundaryconditionsforwave–likeequations,Commun. PureAppl. Math.,Vol.
23,S.707–725,1980
‡‡ A. Bayliss, M. Gunzberger, E. Turkel : Boundary conditions for the numerical solution of elliptic equations in
exteriorregions,SIAMJ.Appl.Math.,Vol. 42,S.430–451,1982
V 19.00.287 PERMASUser’s ReferenceManual(EDU) 4-765
Elements
3D-RBC
(B-T)
4 Element Atlas
TheBayliss–TurkelRBCelementsareavailableuntilnowforstaticelectromagnetic,waveprop-
agation and direct fluid frequency problems. The elements of second order are frequency
dependent for wave propagation and direct fluid frequency problems. For wave problems the
artificial boundaryshould be placed aboutone wavelength away from sources or scatterers to
reduce reflections from the artificial boundary sufficient. Of course this is dependent on the
specified problemandshouldnotbeseenas a constant.
Only isotropic fluid material is applicable to three-dimensional RBC elements, and the appro-
priate material inputtype is GENERAL. The applicable material inputoptions are summarized
in the followingtable:

4.26 Three–Dimensional Engquist–Majda RBC Elements
4.26 Three–Dimensional Engquist–Majda RBC Elements
Overview onAvailableThree–DimensionalEngquist–MajdaRBCElements:
RBCEM1A3 3NodedTriangularElementwith StraightEdges. . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-809
RBCEM1A6 6NodedTriangularElementwith CurvedEdges. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-813
RBCEM1A4 4NodedQuadrilateralElementwith StraightEdges. . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-817
RBCEM1A8 8NodedQuadrilateralElementwith CurvedEdges. . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-821
RBCEM1A9 9NodedQuadrilateralElementwith CurvedEdges. . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-825
RBCEM2A3 3NodedTriangularElementwith StraightEdges. . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-829
RBCEM2A6 6NodedTriangularElementwith CurvedEdges. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-833
RBCEM2A4 4NodedQuadrilateralElementwith StraightEdges. . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-837
RBCEM2A8 8NodedQuadrilateralElementwith CurvedEdges. . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-841
RBCEM2A9 9NodedQuadrilateralElementwith CurvedEdges. . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-845
The RBC (radiation boundary condition) elements are special elements to construct an ar-
tificial boundary and to impose conditions on this surface to simulate an infinite domain. The
Engquist–MajdaRBC elements are based on the one way wave equation approximation tech-
nique. The idea is to permit on an outer boundary only wave motions which are travelling
outward from the range of interest. For further details of the theory see (*) (†). The RBC ele-
ments of first order approximate the pseudo–differential equation with a Taylor approximation
offirstorder,theelementsofsecondorderuseaTaylorapproximationofsecondorder. Ingen-
eraltheelementsofsecondorderaremoreaccuratethanthoseoffirstorder. Onarectangular
boundary,the elementsoffirst orderleadto the Sommerfeldconditionforplanewaves.
The theory of Engquist–Majda used here is based on plane waves. Thus the RBC elements
must be placed onto the surface of a Finite Element mesh which is of rectangular shape only.
With the RBC elements the influence of the unbounded domain is taken into account and the
problemiswellposedtoo. Sonoadditionalboundaryconditionsfortheunboundeddomainare
necessary.
* B. Engquist,A. Majda: Absorbingboundaryconditionsforthe numericalsimulationof waves, Math. Comput.,
Vol.31,S.629–651,1977
† B.Engquist,A.Majda: Radiationboundaryconditionsforacousticandelasticwavecalculations,Commun. Pure
Appl.Math.,Vol. 32,S.312–358,1979
V 19.00.287 PERMASUser’s ReferenceManual(EDU) 4-807
Elements
3D-RBC
(E-M)
4 Element Atlas
The Engquist–Majda RBC elements are available until now for wave propagation and direct
fluid frequency problems. The elements of second order are frequency dependent for wave
propagation and direct fluid frequency problems. For wave problems the artificial boundary
should be placed about one to two wavelengths away from sources or scatterers to reduce
reflections from the artificial boundary sufficient. Of course this is dependenton the specified
problemandshouldnotbeseenas a constant.
Only isotropic fluid material is applicable to three-dimensional RBC elements, and the appro-
priate material inputtype is GENERAL. The applicable material inputoptions are summarized
in the followingtable:

4.27 Axisymmetric Flange Elements
4.27 Axisymmetric Flange Elements
Overview onAvailableAxisymmetric FlangeElements:
RINGX Single-nodeaxisymmetric FlangeElement . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 4-851
The axisymmetric flange elements are displacement models that are fully compatible with the
axisymmetric membrane elements QUAX and TRIAX. Their main application is thus the mod-
elling ofenforcements(flanges,stringers, prestressing cables)in axisymmetric problems.
Unless there is sufficient support by adjacent elements or boundary conditions, the axisym-
metric flange elementsmayintroduce redundantdegreesoffreedomthatmust be suppressed
explicitly.
Allmatrices andforces are with respectto a sector of360degrees(full axisymmetric body).
Axisymmetricflangeelementsmayhave,accordingtotheirnature,onlyhomogeneousisotropic
material, therefore a homogeneousmaterial has to be definedwith TYPE= ISO(default). The
appropriate material property type is GENERAL. All applicable material input options for ax-
isymmetric flangeelementsare summarizedin thefollowingtable:

4.32 Axisymmetric Line Convection Elements
4.32 Axisymmetric Line Convection Elements
Overview onAvailableAxisymmetric Line ConvectionElements:
CONALAX SingleNodeAxisymmetric EdgeConvectionElement . . . . . . . . . . . 4-934
CONLAX SingleNodeAxisymmetric LineConvectionElement. . . . . . . . . . . . 4-939
Axisymmetric line convection elements are used to include convective heat transfer at the
edges of axisymmetric membrane (edge convection) or along axisymmetric flange (line con-
vection) in thermal analysis. In addition, the heat capacity of the convective film may be taken
into account.
Axisymmetric line convection elements are restricted to thermal analysis, and are ignored in
anyotherkind ofanalysis.
Allmatrices andforces are with respectto a sector of360degrees(full axisymmetric body).
If the heat capacity of the convective film should be taken into account, a homogeneous
isotropicmaterialhastobedefinedwithTYPE=ISO (default)andmaterialpropertytypeGEN-
ERAL.Allapplicablematerialinputoptionsforaxisymmetric lineconvectionelementsaresum-
marized in thefollowingtable:

4.35 Axisymmetric Fluid Structure Interface Elements
4.35 Axisymmetric Fluid Structure Interface Elements
Overview onAvailableAxisymmetric Fluid Structure Interface Elements:
FSINTSX3 3NodedCurvedAxisymmetric HarmonicFluidStructure Interface Element4-963
The axisymmetric fluid structure interface elementsare used to couple axisymmetric solid and
fluid domains for coupled analysis. In addition,they may be used to include boundaryabsorp-
tion in the fluiddomain.
Fluid structure interface elements carry displacement degrees of freedom as well as pressure
degree of freedom. For a pure fluid analysis without structure the displacement degrees of
freedomareignored,for a purestructural analysis the interface elementsareignoredatall.
The geometry of axisymmetric elements is fully described by its intersection with the global
r,z-plane where the z-axis is the axis of symmetry (rotational axis for the body of revolution).
Allmatrices andforces refer to a sector of360degrees(full axisymmetric body).
Theorientationofaxisymmetricinterfaceelementsmustbesuchthattheelementnormalpoints
from the fluid to the solid. The local element system for axisymmetric interface elements is
definedasfollows:
1. The m-axis is tangential to the local meridian and points from the edge where the first
′
elementpointis located to thesecond one.
2. Thet-axisistangentialtothecircumferentialdirectionandparalleltotheglobalφ-direction.
′
3. Then-axis is normalto theelementsurface. (m t n) form a right-handsystem.

4.36 Axisymmetric Surface Wave Elements
4.36 Axisymmetric Surface Wave Elements
Overview onAvailableAxisymmetric Surface Wave Elements:
FLWAVEX3 3NodedCurvedAxisymmetric HarmonicSurfaceWave Element. . . . . 4-968
Theaxisymmetricsurfacewaveelementsareusedtoidealizefreesurfacesoftheaxisymmetric
fluid wherethe pressureatthe surface is balancedbythe weightofsurface waves.
Axisymmetric surface waveelementscarry onepressure degreeoffreedom.
Axisymmetric surface wave elements are always placed on the boundary of the fluid perpen-
dicular to the direction of gravity acceleration. The orientation of the element normal is mean-
ingless. The gravity acceleration value itself must be inputted by parameter GFLWAVE within
the system variant,see datablock $PARAMETER, page3-549.
The geometry of axisymmetric elements is fully described by its intersection with the global
r,z-plane where the z-axis is the axis of symmetry (rotational axis for the body of revolution).
Allmatrices andforces refer to a sector of360degrees(full axisymmetric body).
Axisymmetricsurfacewaveelementshaveisotropicfluidmaterial,andonlyfluiddensityisused.
All applicable material input options for axisymmetric surface wave elements are summarized
in the followingtable:

5.1 General
5 Design Element Atlas
Important notice: This chapter provides a detailed description and a complete list of general
purposedesignelementtypes. Foranyothertype pleasereferto 3-62ff.
5.1 General
Fordesignoptimizationpurpose,allpartsofthestructure whichmaybemodifiedareassigned
to so-called Design Elements. They are used to define possible modifications for elements
and nodes belongingto the design element, and are intended for simple and clear description
of interpolation within the design element (interpolation is not yet provided in current version).
Designelementsare usedaccording to followingrules:
• Each design element contains one or more finite elements by unique assignment. To-
getherwith the elements,all nodalpointsconnectedto those elementsare associated to
the designelement.
• Eachdesignelementmayhaveanynumberofdesignvariables,atleastone. Allpossible
modificationswithinthedesignelementaredefineddependentonthosedesignvariables.
• Each design element has a fixed number of design nodes, a defined geometry and cor-
responding interpolation functions. Design nodes are needed for interpolation within the
designelementandshapeoptimizationonly,andmaybe omittedelsewhere.
• Each design element has a fixed type of Geometrical Data Record. For optimal sizing
problemsonlyelementswith matchingGeometricalData Recordmaybeassigned.
• For optimalsizing problemsproperty dependenciesmay be defined for the whole design
element. They are valid for all correspondingfinite elements,independenton its location
within the designelement. Designnodesarenotusedandmaybe omitted.
• For interpolation of properties within the design element, property dependenciesare de-
finedatthedesignnodesofthedesignelement;thenthepropertyisinterpolatedaccord-
ing to the interpolation function of the design element and the location of the element
within the design element. For that case, the design nodes of the design element must
be inputted.
Interpolationofpropertiesis notyet availablein currentversion.
• For shape optimization the coordinates of the design nodes are made dependenton the
design variables,and the coordinatesofall nodalpointsassociated to the corresponding
designelementare modifiedaccording to the designelementinterpolationfunctions.

Verification Results 6 Results
6.1.2 Verification Results Overview
With the GO command in the UCI EXPORT section additional verification results from the
analysis are exported to the postprocessor together with the standard results obtained by the
pure analysisif theDEFAULTswitch VERIFICATIONis setto RESULTS(orON).
Also in UCI sections PRINT and EXPORT those results can be explicitly requested with the
ITEM command.
Selectableresults withoutsetting theVERIFICATIONswitch:
The results below can be printed or exported by an explicit ITEM selection without setting the
VERIFICATIONswitch. Theresults willbeexportedautomatically,if theVERIFICATIONswitch
is set to RESULTSorON andtheyare available.

Contact Results 6 Results
6.1.3 Contact Results Overview
WiththeGOcommandintheUCIEXPORTsectionadditionalresultsfromthecontactanalysis
areexportedtothepostprocessortogetherwiththestandardresultsobtainedbythepurestatic
analysis. Also in UCI sections PRINT and EXPORT those results can be explicitly requested
with the ITEM command. All contact results are based on nodal points, i.e. are scalar values
orvectors atcontact nodes.
According to the solution step in which the data is generated,the contact analysis results may
be separatedin 4 groups:
Scanningresults (verification ofmodel):
Directly after the model’s input and consolidation (e.g. after task scanning with TASKSTORE)
some load-independent* contactresults are availableformodelverification:
INITIAL CONTACT DEFinition
Initial contact definitions with 3-6 scalar valuesper node: the definition counter, the defi-
nition type, the family type of the involved guiding CA-DOFs and, for surface contact, an
isolation-indicator, the patch kink angles before smoothing and an indicator for doubled
contactpairs
INITIAL CONTACT GEOmetry
Itisthenadirvector(geometricalgapvectorfromnodetosurfacenadir)asaresultofthe
neighborhoodsearch
INITIAL CONTACT SYStem
It contains 3 normalized vectors building the axes of the contact system, i.e. the contact
normal(N ) andfrictional y/z (F /F )direction respectively
x y z
Precheck results (verification ofloads):
For a verification of the contact loads the following results are already available after the use
of a STATICTO PRECHECK (hence, may be exported after a test-run without costly calcula-
tions). Of course, the simple STATIC command also includes the precheck. This results are
only exported if explicitly requested (or if the UCI DEFAULT switch VERIFICATION is set to
DEFAULT SET VERIFICATION = RESULTS):
INITIAL CONTACT STATUS
It is a single scalar value for each contact node in each load pattern indicating the geo-
metricalsituationpriortosimulation,i.e. basicallythesignoftheinputgapwidthgivenby
$CONTACTLOAD(see page3-567ff.)
INITIAL GAP [WIDTH]
The initial gap δ is only a signed scalar value of the normal part: open gap if > 0,
0norm
penetrationif < 0
* Inthepost-processortheload-independentresultsmayshowupunderloadpatternzero.

=n.x: Partial/interpolateddependency.
Theresult is notgeneratedif allactive CA-DOFsarelinearly independent.

Theory:
Incontrasttothecalculationofstressesthecalculationofcontactpressureisnotaderivativeof
theelementdisplacements,butisdonebyadirectmappingofthediscretecontactforcestaking
into account the areas and shape-functions of the neighboring element faces. This approach
hasseveraladvantages:
• Contact pressure is available for all element faces, i.e. even for elements which do not
have anyelasticity in normaldirection (e.g. shell,membraneorplotelements).
V 19.00.287 PERMASUser’s ReferenceManual(EDU) 6-33
Results
Contact Pressure 6 Results
• Contact pressure is also available for rigid surfaces, e.g. for elements with suppress,
prescribed ordependentnodes.
• Uniqueseparationofnormalandtangentialpressure for nodeswith multiplecontacts.
• Pressure values are calculated at the contact nodes directly (no gauss point extrapola-
tion).
Remarks
1. The area-related contact pressure and shear result use as reference surface all element
faces moistened by the corresponding contact definition. I.e. the reference surface is
derived from the adjacent finite-element mesh and not taken from a surface definition
usedin the contactdefinition!
This makes the reference surface independentof the contactdefinitiontype, so that this
area-relatedresults areavailablefor simplenodalpointcontactsaswellasforbothsides
ofa surface-to-nodeorsurface-to-surface contact!
For line-like contacts the length of the moistened element edges are multiplied by the
valueoftheUCIswitch CALINEWIDTH(default1.0)to getareferencearea. Forsingular
node-to-node contacts the value of UCI switch CAPOINTAREA is taken as a reference
area(default0.0).
2. For incompatible meshes an additional balancing between both sides of contact is ap-
plied, taking into account the local mesh size. For equally sized meshes this means just
an average determination, but for ample different meshes local details of the finer side
arenotsmearedbya coarse partnermesh.
3. Contact forces as well as contact pressure often show very high gradients at the border
ofthecontactregion–especiallyatgeometricalsharpedges(edgepressure). Thisisnot
a simulation or discretization error, but meets the correct progression also known from
analytical press-fit solutions. Depending on the geometrical characterstics a very fine
meshing of a sharp edge might even lead to singular effects with almost infinite stress
values.†
4. The direct mapping algorithm used for the calculation of area-related contact results is
suited for elements with linear, quadratic or incomplete quadratic shape functions. How-
ever, mixed-case elements with a linear shape function in normal and a quadratic shape
function in tangential direction (i.e. thick shell elements TRIMS6 and QUAMS8/9 or
quadratic gasket elements GKPNT15/18and GKHEX20/27)may show a slightly discon-
tinuouspressuredistributionfrommidtocornernodes–similartothenon-smoothcontact
forces atquadraticshapedelements.
5. Atthesymmetryborderofcyclicsymmetricmodelsonlyonehalfoftheeffectivereference
areacanbederivedfromthecontactadjacentelementfaces(thesecondhalfactsviathe
† Inpraxisedgesofrealpartsmostlyshowsmallroundingsorpeakstressvaluesatsharpedgesareloweredby
microscopic small areas of plastification wihtout affecting the part’s function. Hence, for the outer most series
ofnodalpointsitisoftenacceptabletotolerateaSTATICcontactpressureabovethematerial’slimitofelasticity
withoutthisdemandingamoreexpensiveNLMATERIALcalculation.

symmetry-joins on the other side of the symmetry plane, but without direct connectivity
to the contact nodes). Therefore contact nodes at the border of cyclic symmetry usually
showa doubledcontactpressure althoughthe contactforces are correct.
Standard symmetry is not impaired by this effect. Notwithstanding contact pairs along
the border of this symmetry also see only half the effective reference area, but as the
very same nodesalso getonly halfthe contact forces this effect is compensatedandthe
contact pressure attheborderofsymmetry is correct, too.

6.2 Result Items Contact Status
If anodeis partofseveralcontact definitionsthe finalstatus valueis buildby adecimalcoding
of all corresponding contact status. The status values are collected in descending order with
the decimal point after the first status value. E.g. if an edge node participates in 2 contact
definitions, one of them passive (status 1) and the other one slipping (status 4) then the final
contactstatus ofthatnodewillbeCA-Status=4.1 !
As surface contact allows the contact between incompatible meshes each node on a surface
maybe influencedby several(partiallyinherited)status values:
• The primary contact status value reflects the contact situation directly at the node’s loca-
tion, e.g. contact of node with a patch of the opposing surface (i.e. the standard contact
status atthatnode).†
• Asurface nodemayinheritanadditionalsecondarycontactstatusfrom thenearestnadir
point of an ’opponent’ contact node.* Optionally this secondary contact status may
be shifted with -0.5 by setting the UCI switch CASURFST=SHIFT, see page 2-33. This
setting helpsto clearly distinguish betweenprimaryandsecondarystatusvalues.
• If a contact node is part of a surface-to-surface contact definition this node will show the
maximum valueofthe primaryandsecondarystatus.
• Moreover all orphan contact nodes, i.e. contact nodes for which no contact partner was
found (see also isolation type) get a status value of 0.0. Nodes not belonging to any
contact definitionwillgetnostatus value.
FigureF6-5: ContactStatusforexampleCA4(surface-to-node).
† Asurfacenodeinasurface-to-nodecontacthasnoprimarystatus.
* Thedistanceuptowhichasecondarycontactfromapatchcontributestoanode’scontactstatusiscontrolledby
theUCIswitchCASURFMSR,seepage2-33.

4. Slip force declinationangle
The Coulomb friction law prescribes the direction of the frictional force relative to slip
displacement vector. The value of the slip force declination angle shows the declination
of the frictional force from its direction calculated based on the slip displacement vector.
Forisotropic friction law the declinationanglecan befoundas
∠( R ,r ) (E6-4)
slip slip
−
I.e. the frictional force must pointin an opposite direction to the slip displacementvector.
It doesnotholdfor theorthotropicfriction !
Ideally,thevalueofthedeclinationmustbezero. Notethatforthesmallforceordisplace-
ment values (with values close to an accuracy limit), the directions can be only badly
defined. In such cases for the very accurate solution,the declination valuescan bequite
large.

imal coding of all corresponding definition types. The definition types are collected in
descending order with the decimal point after the first status value. E.g. if an edge node
participates in 2 contact definitions, in one of them on the node side (value 2) and in the
other one on the surface side (value 1) then the final definition type of that node will be
2.1 !

6.2 Result Items Initial Contact Geometry
6.2.65 Initial Contact Geometry
Initial geometricalgapvector
• Type: Nadirvectoratcontact nodes (load-independentresult)
• Available aftermodelconsolidation(e.g. aftertask scanning withTASKSTORE)
• ResultLabel: UCAGEO0
• GENERATE: n/a (automaticallygenerated)
• EXPORT: ITEM INITIAL CONTACT GEOMETRY
• ExportRule: DefaultResult
• POST,HDF: $DATAINICAGEO,INITIAL CONTACT GEOMETRY
• PRINT: ITEM INITIAL CONTACT GEOMETRY
• XYDATA: n/a
• RelatedDATkeywords: $CONTACT
The initial contact geometry shows the nadir vectors i.e. the geometrical gap vectors from
the contact nodes to their corresponding surface nadir obtained by the neighborhood search.
Hence, the nadir vectors and the normal direction of the contact system are collinear and the
lengthofthe nadirvector isidenticalto the absolutevalueofthe geometricalgapwidth.*

SPR 6 Results
6.3 Theory
6.3.1 SPR Procedure
SPR: Smooth Patch Recovery method,
[Zienkiewicz].
• Evaluate stress at “superconvergent”
points.
• Buildelementpatches:
For each interior corner node an element
patch is build consisting of those ele-
integration point
ments sharing this corner node, which is
superconvergent point
denoted the patch node. Patch nodes element patch
must not be located on boundaries, on patch node
propertyinterfacesoronmeshinterfaces.
• Leastsquarefit:
To approximate the stress inside the
patch a polynomialstress ansatz is used.
The polynomial coefficients are deter-
minedviaaleastsquarefittothestresses y
atthe“superconvergent”points. x
• Nodalvaluesfrom patches:
The nodal stress values are determined
asarithmetic meanof the evaluatedpoly-
nomials from the contributing patches.
Each SPR patch contributes to its interior
nodes. Ifthepatchincludesboundaryno-
desit also contributes to thisnodes.
Inordertohaveconsistentpatches,themodelhastobepartitionedduetocertainrules. Thisis
performedinternallywithintheSPRcomputationsothatnomanualactionisneeded. However,
some settingsare availableto influencethe automaticSPRmodelpartitioning.
• No SPR patch nodes at MPC interfaces, i.e. MPC interfaces are treated like exterior
boundaries regarding the SPR procedure. Hence, e.g. at an MPC ISURFACE between
a HEXE8 and TET10 volume mesh, SPR stresses will be generated for both volume
meshesseparately. I.e. there willbe noSPRpatch with HEXE8andTET10elements.
• Splitmodeldueto elementfamilies.
• Materialbordersare also separators(except e.g. shortfibre materials).
DEFAULT SET SPRMATDEC = ON

6.3.2 Absolute Error Indicator (AEI)
The Absolute Error Indicator (AEI) σ is a scalar measure of the discretization error in terms
AEI
ofstress withinoneelement. It is definedas
σ = max σ σ ,
AEI FE SPR
V k − k
where V denotes the element volume, σ is the standard element stress and σ the SPR
FE SPR
stress. The stress difference is measured in the Frobeniusnorm A = √A: A. Because the
k k
AEI is based on the SPR stress the same restrictions apply regarding mesh partitioning and
boundaries.
V 19.00.287 PERMASUser’s ReferenceManual(EDU) 6-199
Results
AEI 6 Results
The AEI is an indicator for the discretization error in terms of stress and must not be mixed
up with the exact error in the stress. The purpose of the AEI is to identify those mesh regions
where the mesh quality should be improved and/or the mesh should be refined in order to
reduce the error in the stresses. Note that at stress singularities like at corners, the error will
notbereducedbya mesh refinement.
Example example LS19 on page 2-243 ff. of [um550] shows an application of SPR stresses
andthe AEI.

7.1 General
7.1 General
Default result item selection
The export process has a default result selection rule in order to avoid explicit selections for
manycases. Therule is asfollowing:
1. Primary results arealwaysselected.
2. Eachsecondaryresultwhichisgeneratedexplicitlyisselectedasfarasthepostprocessor
isabletosupporttheitem. (Exceptionsaredocumentedinthecorrespondingoutputdoor
sections.)
3. Verification item if "DEFAULT SET MODEL = verification" is selected. Verification item
shouldonlybe usedfor testing purposein conjunctionwith TASKSTORE.
Explicit result item selections
Using the EXPORT ITEM (see page 2-373 ff.) command, further selections may be done in
addition to the default selection. If only explicit selections are desired, the default selection
mustbe clearedpreviously.
7.1.1 Naming rule for Export Files
The naming convention for the postprocessing files is designed to be as common for the dif-
ferent postprocessors as possible. The specific naming rules are documented for each post-
processor separately. Of course, the names are machine dependent. Some restrictions are
documentedforeach postprocessor,too.
Thereareseveral parametersinfluencingtheresult file names:
1. Project name
2. Component(in case ofsubstructuring)
3. Situation(if several variantsare used)
4. Exportmode(direct/combined)
5. Exportedresult item (forseveral postprocessors)
6. Task loop

7.2 Export to PERMAS
7.2.1 General
Model and result output can be generated in the EXPORT (see page 2-363 ff.) section of
PERMAS.ThegeneratedoutputiswritteninPERMAS(ref. chapter3)inputformat. Therefore
this output may be used as model/result input for a subsequent PERMAS run or for other
postprocessing purposes.
Foreasyprocessing the outputfile is written in a fixed format.
Thestructure offile is asfollowing:
!#------------------------------------------------------------------------------
!# Result file written by PERMAS Version xversxxx
!# Distributed by INTES GmbH Stuttgart
!# Date: xxdatexx xxtimexx
!#..............................................................................
!# P r o j e c t
!# xxprojxx
!#..............................................................................
!# Site: xxcustomerxx
!# Host: xxhostname / xxosnamexx
!# Code: xxportxx
!#------------------------------------------------------------------------------
$ENTER COMPONENT NAME = LS1 DOFTYPE = DISP MATH
!#-----------------------< Variant information block >--------------------------
!#
!# Conf.: xxxxxxxxxxxx Comp.: xxxxxxxxxxxx Sit.: xxxxxxxxxxxx
!# Analysis type: xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx
!#
!#------------------------------------------------------------------------------
$RESULTS NAME = xxxxxxxxxxxx
$PARAMETER
ANALYSIS = ’xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx’
$DATA xxxitemxxxxx
& xxxlabelxxxx = 1
!#------------------------< Data item description >---------------------------
!# Data Object: xxxxxxxxxxxx TEXT: xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx
!# LINES = 999999999
!# FORMAT (1X,I9,4(1X,1PE13.6),/,100(10X,4(1X,1PE13.6),/))
!#----------------------------------------------------------------------------
1 0.000000E+00 0.000000E+00 0.000000E+00
2 -4.761904E-05 -4.566747E-04 0.000000E+00
. . .
. . .
$END RESULTS
$EXIT COMPONENT
$FIN

7.2.4 Binary File Framework
HDFDataModel
• TheHDFformat hastwoprimary objects
Group : is like a directoryofa file system
Dataset : is like a file ofa file system
• andAttributes to annotatedata.
Eachresultitemis storedin aHDFGroupnamedaccordingto theitem name,e.g. ’ELEMENT
STRESS’ and may contain several HDF Datasets corresponding to e.g. LPATs or xy-curves.
All result items belong to a HDF Group named like the situation they belong to. This group is
theSituationGroup. ThesituationbelongstoaHDFGroupaccordingtothecomponentname,
and if the model has a multilevel configuration, this component belongs to a HDF Group with
the configuration(top component)name.
/.File Header
/[configuration/]component/
/[configuration/]component/situation/
/[configuration/]component/situation/.Analysis
/[configuration/]component/situation/.Model
/[configuration/]component/situation/item
/[configuration/]component/situation/item/.ColDes
/[configuration/]component/situation/item/.RowDes
/[configuration/]component/situation/item/Column1
/[configuration/]component/situation/item/Column2
/[configuration/]component/situation/item
/[configuration/]component/situation/item/.Abscissae
/[configuration/]component/situation/item/.Label
/[configuration/]component/situation/item/Curve1
Thereisa ’.File Header’HDFDatasetin the HDFRootGroupofthe binaryfile. Thisdatasetis
written as a ’string’ datatypewith a fixed lengthof80 characters andseveral lines.
The SituationGroup containsone additionalHDFDataset named’.Analysis’. Thisdataset is a
’string’ datatype with a fixed length of 40 characters, containing the analysis command of the
situation,e.g. ’STATIC’.ItcanalsocontainthePostprocessingModelasaHDFDatasetnamed
’.Model’.
Each right-hand side of a result item is stored in a HDF Dataset named ’Columni’ with the
column index i of the item. The value (e.g. LPAT, TIME or FREQUENCY) of the Column is
stored in the HDF Dataset ’.ColDes’ at the position i. The label of the result position (node,
element,...) is stored in the HDFDataset’.RowDes’.
V 19.00.287 PERMASUser’s ReferenceManual(EDU) 7-21
PERMAS Export
to
7 Export Formats
If an item consists of curves, the ordinate values are stored in a HDF Dataset named ’Curvei’
withthecurveindexi. ThelabelofthecurveisstoredintheHDFDataset’.Label’attheposition
i. The independent values (e.g. LPAT, TIME or FREQUENCY) of the Curve are stored in the
HDFDataset’.Abscissae’.
The description of the dimensions and the dimensionality is done in FORTRAN notation. The
indices startwith 1,andthe first indexis runningfastest.
EachresultHDFDatasetisatwodimensionalarrayforrealdataandathreedimensionalarray
in the case of complex data. The result data components (e.g. DOFs) are stored in the first
dimension and the datapoints (nodes, elements, ...) in the second dimension of the real data
array. Complex values are stored as real and imaginary part of the complex data in the first
dimensionofthethreedimensionalarray. Theresultdatacomponentsarestoredinthesecond
dimension and the datapoints are stored in the third dimension of the three dimensional data
array.
All nodal point results and element results with result data at elements or result data at center
of elements have a HDF Dataset ’.RowDes’ which is a vector with the nodal point IDs or the
elementIDs. Thevaluesare 64bitvalues.
The column description HDF Dataset ’.ColDes’ is a vector with load pattern IDs, column IDs,
time values, frequencies or a text description. The values are 64 bit values, the strings have a
fixed length.

Rowpackrule attributes
CodeC2 : This attribute contains the row pack rule for ’.RowDes’ column 2 (e.g. 2.3.2.5). It
is a decimal coded value with following meaning described from right to left. Each
field showsthe width of its decimalportion. The ’Most Right’ value ’Pos 1’ must be
usedtogetthecorrectdatalength. Theothervaluescanbeusedfordisplayingthe
data.
Pos1: Thisportionis(inthisexample)5digitswideandholdsthenumberofvalues
for thiselement.
Pos2: This portion is (in this example) 2 digits wide and holds the dimension of
ONEdatapoint,e.g. 6for Tensor,3 forvector, 1 forscalar.
Pos3: This portion is (in this example)3 digits wide and holds the numberof layer
orZEROif notlayered.
Pos4: This portion is (in this example)2 digits wide and holds the data pointcode
for datadisplay.
0 : Noexplicit position
1 : Dataatcenterofelement
2 : Dataatelementnodes
3 : Dataatlayer center
4 : Dataatalllayer for allnodes
5 : Dataatallnodesfor alllayer
