7.2.7 Output Format
The lines of the PERMAS output file are written in a fixed format. Therefore each line may be
processed with a specific format.
Someusefulinformationare givenascommentlinesstarting with "!#."
The following format descriptions are in the sense of FORTRAN format statements. For other
programminglanguagesthe appropriatedefinitionsmustbeused.
General information block
!#-----------------------< General information block >--------------------------
!#
!# Result file written by PERMAS xversxxx on xxmachinexxxxxxx
!# Project: xxprojxxxxxx at xxdatexxxxxx/xtimexxx
!#
!#------------------------------------------------------------------------------
PERMAS Version number and machine

V 19.00.287 PERMASUser’s ReferenceManual(EDU) 7-333
PERMAS Export
to
7 Export Formats
C*($) RDLINE ........RDLINE ........RDLINE ........RDLINE ........
SUBROUTINE RDLINE (IUNIT,FORM,NLINES,NCOL,
* N O P O E L , D A T A , L I N E , E N D )
C--X--------------------------------------------------------------------
C # Entry # to Permas 5 Data file processing
C
C Read one data line from result file
C
C --> IUNIT : FORTRAN unit number
C --> FORM : Format specification
C --> NLINES : Number of lines to process
C --> NCOL : Number of columns in data line
C <-- NOPOEL : Nodal point or element number
C <-- DATA : Numerical values
C <-- LINE : Last line if end of block was found (character*80)
C <-- END : .TRUE. if end of data line was found
C-----------------------------------------------------------------------
C (C) Copyright INTES GmbH, Stuttgart, Germany
C!-----------------------------------------------
CHARACTER*(*) FORM,LINE
LOGICAL END
DIMENSION DATA(*)
CHARACTER*80 LINES(100)
C-----------------------------------------------------------------------
C
C ... Read in line and test for end of block
READ(IUNIT,’(A80)’)LINES(1)
IF( LINES(1)(1:1) .EQ. ’$’)THEN
END = .TRUE.
LINE = LINES(1)
GOTO 999
ENDIF
C
C Next line found get rest of data
IF( NLINES .GT. 1 )THEN
DO 10 I=2,NLINES
READ(IUNIT,’(A80)’)LINES(I)
10 CONTINUE
ENDIF
C
C Convert data
READ(LINES,FORM)NOPOEL,(DATA(I),I=1,NCOL)
END = .FALSE.
C----
999 CONTINUE
RETURN
END

ot
tropxE
SAMREP
7.2 Export to PERMAS
C*($) RDBLOC ........RDBLOC ........RDBLOC ........RDBLOC ........
SUBROUTINE RDBLOC (IUNIT,
* N A M O B J , T E X T , L I N E S , F O R M )
C--X--------------------------------------------------------------------
C # Entry # to Permas 5 Data file processing
C
C Get information from data comment block
C
C --> IUNIT : FORTRAN unit with connected input file
C <-- NAMOBJ: Name of data object
C <-- TEXT : Description text from data object
C <-- LINES : Number of lines for one data item
C <-- FORM : Fortran format to convert data
C-----------------------------------------------------------------------
C (C) Copyright INTES GmbH, Stuttgart, Germany
C!-----------------------------------------------
CHARACTER*(*) NAMOBJ,TEXT,FORM
CHARACTER INAM*13,ITEXT*40,FFORM*65
C-----------------------------------------------------------------------
C
NAMOBJ = ’ ’
TEXT = ’ ’
FORM = ’ ’
C
C Get book name and text
READ(IUNIT,’(16X,A13,7X,A40)’)INAM,ITEXT
NAMOBJ = INAM
TEXT = ITEXT
C
C Get number of lines
READ(IUNIT,’(11X,I9)’)LINES
C
C Get format for data line
READ(IUNIT,’(10X,A65)’)FFORM
FORM = FFORM
C
C Skip next line
READ(IUNIT,’(A65)’)FFORM
C----
RETURN
END

PRESsure USR Nodal point pressures/mode shapes, eigenvalues and damping ma-
trices.
Remarks:
1. The eigenvaluesand eigenmodescan be exported after a (Fluid) Vibration Analysis or a
(Fluid)ModalFrequencyAnalysis. Theeigenmodesofthemodalfrequencyanalysismay
containrigid bodymodesorcontstantpressure modes.
2. Thedampingmatrices can be exportedaftera (Fluid)ModalFrequencyAnalysis.

OAV
7.9 Export to VAO
UGVFile Format
The UGV File is a binary file with a maximum size of 2 GByte. The first five words are the file
descriptor.
1. MagicID (is currently 948250943)
2. VAO version (is currently 2)
3. Numberofdataforeach nodalpoint(numberofplanes). Is6 for displacementsand1for
pressures.
4. Numberofnodalpointson UGVfile
5. NumberofmodesonUGV file
The UGV file is written in several parts, if the total size of the modes is larger than 2 GB. All
files contains all modes of a number of nodes. The matrix is split in row direction on the UGV
files. TheextensionsareUGV1,UGV2...UGVi.
GRID FileFormat
Field-1 Field-2 Field-3 Field-4 Field-5 Field-6 Field-7 Field-8 Field-9
GRID ID CP X X X CD PS SEID
1 2 3
DataItems:
ID 1 000000>I>0 UniquenodalpointID
CP Integer 0 Coordinatesystem ID (alwaysblank)
≥
X thru X Real Nodalpointlocation
1 3
CD Integer 0 Displacementcoordinatesystem ID (always blank)
≥
PS I 0 orblank Permanentsingle–pointconstraint (alwaysblank)
≥
SEID I 0 orblank SuperelementID (alwaysblank)
≥
Example:
GRID* 2 0.000000E+00 0.000000E+00
0.000000E+00
GRID* 3 0.100000E+01 0.000000E+00

7.11.4 Static correction modes
Aslongasmodalsynthesis(Craig-Bamptonmethod)isnotsupportedinPERMASthefollow-
ing procedureis usedfor generatingstatic correction modesforADAMSinterface.
• Staticcorrectionmodesarecalculatedfordegreeoffreedomwhicharedeclared$EXTERNAL
(see page3-109ff.)
ForthecalculationofelasticmodesinasinglecomponentEXTERNALdegreesoffreedomare
fixed. Thereforetheresult is thesame asif thedegreesoffreedomare SUPPRESSED.
Restriction
Thefollowingrestriction must berespected forthe calculation ofstatic correction modes:
• No substructuring is supported
• No constraint variantfor EXTERNALdegreesoffreedom possible ( EXTERNALdeclara-
tion belongsto thebasic moduleofthe component)
• Calculationofstatic correction modesis donebythe ADAMSinterface

8.1 Degree of Anisotropy
8 Material Description (Theory)
8.1 Degree of Anisotropy
The degree of anisotropy is a fundamental property of all types of material. In many practical
applications the material behavior can be considered as isotropic and only few constants are
needed to describe it, but some types of material, e.g. fiber-reinforced plastics, wood or rein-
forced concrete show a distinct anisotropic behavior which has to be taken into account. The
descriptionofgeneralanisotropicbehaviorisanexpensivetask,soe.g. fortheconstitutivema-
trix C which relates stresses and strains in linear elasticity twenty-one independentconstants
are needed. Fortunately most anisotropic materials have any planes of symmetry for their be-
havior, reducing the number of independentconstants and so the amount of work to describe
it. For user convenience different types of anisotropic behavior are implemented in PERMAS,
identifiedby theirso-called degreeofanisotropy.
The simplest case is isotropic material behavior. No dependency on orientation of material in
space exists, thereis aninfinite numberofplanesofmaterialpropertysymmetry.
In contrast, if there is not anyplane of material property symmetry, the material is called (gen-
eral)anisotropicortriclinic.
If thereis onlyoneplaneofmaterialpropertysymmetry the materialiscalled monoclinic.
If there are two orthogonalplanes of material property symmetry, symmetry will exist also rel-
ative to a third mutually orthogonal plane. The intersections of the three planes define the
principal directions of the material. Using the principal directions to establish the stress-strain
relationleadsto a so-called orthotropicmaterial.
If there is one plane in which all material properties are equal in all directions the material is
called transversely isotropic.

8.5 Heat Capacity
8.5 Heat Capacity
Theamountofheatrequiredtoraisetheunitvolumeofthematerialby1degreeintemperature
is called heatcapacity perunit volume κ, andis used in transient thermalanalysis. Since heat
capacity is a scalar quantity, the input does not depend on the degree of anisotropy of the
material.
Heat capacity may be a function of temperature. For each kind of homogeneousmaterial one
heat capacity value or one heat capacity function may be input, using the data block header
$HEATCAP.
